linux-cleanup is a Bash command-line utility that reclaims disk space on Linux by deleting regenerable caches — package-manager caches, browser caches, build-tool caches, unused Android emulator images, stale node_modules directories, and system journals. It is aimed at developer machines, where tens of gigabytes of this material accumulates without anyone noticing. It is a destructive tool. Every deletion is permanent, and there is no undo. Its safety comes from refusing to touch the wrong things in the first place, not from being able to put them back. This tool deletes files permanently There is no undo, no trash, no backup step, and no --dry-run flag. Deleted data is gone unless you have your own backup. Read What it deletes and run the read-only preview before you let it remove anything. Finding the big, boring wins. Yarn, npm and pnpm caches routinely hold 10–30 GB on a machine that has been building projects for a year. Not deleting the wrong thing. A path allowlist hard-refuses ~/Documents, ~/.ssh, ~/.config, /etc and friends, after symlink resolution. Leaving recently-used files alone. Since 1.2.0 the default is to prune, not wipe: within a cache, only files untouched for 100+ days are removed. See the staleness gate. Telling you what it did. Every session writes a JSON report and a log naming every path it touched. Staying offline. No network code path exists. Nothing leaves your machine unless you email it.

Being clear about the boundaries is more useful than a feature list. Not a backup tool. It deletes; it never archives. Nothing it removes is recoverable from within the tool. Not a dry-run-first tool. There is no --dry-run flag. The read-only mode is a separate command, --scan, and it is on you to run it. Not a security scanner. It will not find secrets, malware, or vulnerabilities. Not cross-platform. Linux only. The npm package declares "os": ["linux"]. Not fully cross-distro. Cache cleanup inside $HOME works anywhere, but the --system mode is Debian/Ubuntu only — it calls apt and dpkg directly. Not a substitute for your judgement. Read what it proposes before you confirm it.

Developer machines accumulate an enormous amount of regenerable junk — package-manager caches measured in tens of gigabytes, browser caches, build-tool caches, emulator images, and node_modules for projects abandoned two years ago. Existing cleaners tended to fall into one of two shapes. Either they did not know about modern developer caches at all, or they were single-button wipers that deleted whatever looked like junk and hoped for the best. linux-cleanup takes the opposite stance: scriptable, transparent, allowlist-guarded, and interactive by default. You can read exactly what it will touch before it touches anything.

Fail closed. An allowlist, not a blocklist. A path the tool does not recognise is refused. A blocklist puts one typo between clearing a cache and clearing a home directory. Distinguish caches from tools. ~/.cache/yarn regenerates in seconds; a Gradle wrapper distribution is a 230 MB download you might need next month. The staleness gate exists because treating those the same was wrong, and 1.2.0 changed it. The user is the oracle for personal data. Nothing on disk distinguishes an installer you will never open again from the only copy of a document. The tool refuses to guess, which is why those modes ignore --yes. Prevention over recovery. No undo, by choice — an undo log is write amplification on the disk you are freeing, and it breeds carelessness. Auditable over convenient. Bash, because it is already installed and can be read. A compiled binary would be more ergonomic and much harder to trust. No network, ever. No telemetry, no analytics, no update check. Nothing leaves your machine unless you email it.

Two of the safety features exist because someone pointed out a real problem. The protected install-root list came from a genuine defect: pnpm cleanup targeted ~/.local/share/pnpm — the install root — and removed globally installed packages. Fixed in 1.1.0, along with an assertion so it cannot recur. The staleness gate came from a user observing that 1.2.0 still wiped Android AVDs wholesale, and that the same reasoning should apply to anything that is a tool rather than a cache. That became 1.2.1. If you find something wrong, say so.

A "Full documentation" section in the README linking the most-used pages. Code, safety guards and the CLI surface are unchanged from 1.3.0.
Final-polish release: a visual menu and automatic crash capture. No new cleanup logic; existing safety guards and staleness gates unchanged.

TUI mode (-t / --tui / -g / --gui) — a whiptail or dialog driven menu. Each selection drops back to normal CLI output for the run, then returns to the menu. Falls back gracefully to the CLI menu when neither tool is installed, with a per-distro install hint. Automatic crash-bundle capture — an EXIT trap that, on an unexpected non-zero exit, writes a self-contained crash-<stamp>.tar.gz to ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/ holding the session log, the most recent record and a system manifest, then prints a one-liner you can email. Suppressed on clean exit, Ctrl-C (130), SIGTERM (143) and argument-parse exits (2). No network calls — the bundle stays on your machine until you choose to share it. A TUI About dialog carrying version, contact details, licence and the privacy guarantee.
Banner and session-summary suppression now includes tui mode, so the dialog is not fighting log output.
Minor bug fixes and internal stability improvements.

Extends the 1.2.0 staleness gate to anything that is a tool rather than a regenerable cache. Such deletions now require both that no active software depends on the asset and that you have not touched it in --days days.

Android AVDs — previously wiped ~/.android/avd wholesale on confirm. Now each *.avd directory is inspected as a unit, paired with its sibling *.ini, and pruned only when every file in the profile is idle past the threshold. Recently-used emulator profiles survive intact. VS Code / Cursor superseded extensions — the "a newer version exists" check covered the first condition; the superseded directory must now also be idle past the threshold. Recently-loaded older versions are listed but kept, with per-version idle days shown. Flatpak user data — ~/.local/share/flatpak holds installed user-scope apps, not just caches. The module now refuses to touch the tree if any user-scope app is installed, and additionally requires the tree to be idle past the threshold. Points at flatpak uninstall --user --unused for the safer path.

newest_access_age_days <path> — returns days since the freshest atime/mtime anywhere under a path. prune_stale_units <root> <days> [glob] — treats each top-level child as indivisible, so a partial prune cannot corrupt state.

A user pointed out that 1.2.0 still wiped Android AVDs wholesale, and that the same reasoning should apply to anything that is a tool rather than a cache: do not remove software another tool depends on, and do not remove software the user themselves used recently.
The default delete strategy became stale-only. Nothing inside a target cache is removed unless its files have been untouched — both atime and mtime — for --days days, default 100.

clean_target, the shared cleaner behind every cache module, now prunes rather than full-wipes. It deletes only files past the threshold, then sweeps empty directories. Recently-used files survive and the directory shell stays so tools still find their layout. --all-safe prunes per target the same way, and its summary reports bytes freed and bytes kept per target. npm cache cleanup honours the staleness gate instead of always running npm cache clean --force, which ignored age entirely. The pre-run banner states the active strategy — "prune ≥Nd" or "FULL PURGE".

--purge-all restores pre-1.2.0 wipe-everything behaviour, documented with the trade-off spelled out. prune_stale <root> <days> — a public helper for modules that refuses protected paths, deletes only where both timestamps exceed the threshold, sweeps empty directories, and reports bytes freed.

The 1.1.0 default deleted whole cache trees on confirm. That was right for ~/.cache/yarn, which regenerates quickly, and wrong for ~/.gradle/wrapper/dists/ — a 230 MB download you might genuinely need next month. A 100-day threshold cleanly separates "I touched this recently and would miss it" from "I have not opened this in three months". Power users can still force the old behaviour or sharpen the gate with -d 30.
Safety-hardening release. Closes the door on globally installed packages and shell-init files ever being touched.

pnpm globals were being wiped. Cleanup of the pnpm content store targeted ~/.local/share/pnpm (PNPM_HOME) — which holds globally installed packages, bin shims, and the pnpm binary itself from pnpm setup. It now targets only ~/.local/share/pnpm/store, the regenerable content-addressable cache. Affected --all-safe, menu option 3, scan, walkthrough and --list-targets.

PROTECTED_EXACT — an exact-match block on package-manager install directories and runtime homes: pnpm, npm, yarn, bun, deno, volta, nvm, fnm, cargo, rustup and Go. PROTECTED_BASENAMES — refuses any path whose basename is a shell-init or history file, regardless of its location. An --all-safe startup assertion that aborts with a BUG: message if any protected runtime directory ever leaks into the target list, preventing a silent regression.
bun: cache cleanup at ~/.bun/install/cache; ~/.bun/install/global protected. deno: cache cleanup at ~/.cache/deno; ~/.deno/bin protected. Both wired into --all-safe, --scan and the new globals audit.

--globals — a read-only audit listing directly-installed global packages from npm, pnpm, yarn, bun and deno, marking each recently used, needed by: <pkg>, or STALE — safe to uninstall, and printing copy-pasteable uninstall commands. Never deletes anything. Works even when the package manager CLI is not on PATH. --doctor — detects a runtime present on disk but not wired into shell init (nvm, pnpm, bun, deno, cargo) and offers to append the canonical block. Appends only, with confirmation. Never deletes or modifies existing lines.
--all-safe prints explicit "globals are PRESERVED" and "shell-init files are NEVER touched" notices.
Initial public release.

Published to npm — runnable via npx linux-cleanup or npm install -g linux-cleanup. The package ships a thin Node launcher that locates the bash entry point and routes logs and records to ~/.linux-cleanup/ so they survive npx temp eviction. Direct git clone also supported, keeping output inside the clone.

Guided ten-step walkthrough as the default mode, with progress headers, a / s / q prompts, per-step bytes-freed display and a running total. Allowlist-based safety — refuses any path inside a curated protected list, plus bare $HOME and /. Personal data interactive-only — never batched, never --yes-able. Cleanup categories — package-manager caches (yarn, npm, pnpm, pip, composer); application caches (Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Chromium, Edge, Vivaldi, Gradle, Cypress, Playwright, TypeScript, Zoom); developer tools (Android AVDs, pub-cache, Dart, flatpak); editor extensions; stale node_modules; partial downloads and stale personal files; system cleanup under sudo. Session records — canonical JSON written every run, with on-demand Markdown and HTML export. HTML uses dark-mode-aware embedded CSS. Reports manager (--reports) and non-interactive --export FMT ID. Self-test (--self-test) verifying dependencies, the syntax of every shell file, and safety-guard sanity — asserting protection returns true for /, $HOME, ~/Documents and /etc. --feedback and --debug-bundle for structured bug reporting. Privacy — zero network calls. No telemetry, analytics or crash reporting. The only data that leaves your machine is what you choose to email. Credits in every artefact — logs open with a self-attributing header, records carry a top-level credits block, HTML output is footer-credited. Setup helpers — --install-alias, --install-cron and their uninstall counterparts. NO_COLOR support and --no-color.

HTML output escapes all JSON-derived values through jq's @html filter, preventing injection from a malformed record. command -v guards on every optional dependency (snap, crontab, xdg-open, jq). realpath -m resolves symlinks before any protected-path check, so a symlink cannot evade the allowlist.
The authoritative changelog lives in the source repository.
Cache cleanup inside $HOME works on every Linux distribution. That is the large majority of what the tool reclaims. The exception is --system, which is Debian and Ubuntu only.

Distro family $HOME cache cleanup --system Debian, Ubuntu, Mint, Pop!_OS Full Full Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma Full Partial — apt steps fail Arch, Manjaro, EndeavourOS Full Partial — apt steps fail openSUSE Full Partial — apt steps fail Alpine, minimal containers Needs GNU coreutils Partial — apt steps fail WSL (any distro) Full As the underlying distro --system has no distro detection The apt steps call apt and dpkg directly, with no command -v guard and no fallback to dnf, pacman or zypper. On a non-Debian system they fail with "command not found" per step. The mode does not abort — it moves to the next step — so on Fedora or Arch you get the journal, /tmp and page-cache steps working and the package steps failing noisily. Nothing is damaged; the reclaim is simply smaller than advertised. Some descriptions of this tool claim graded multi-distro support for --system, with dnf substituting for apt and paccache on Arch. No such code exists. Verify with grep -rn 'dnf\|pacman\|zypper' modules/system_sudo.sh on a clone — it returns nothing.

--system step Debian/Ubuntu Fedora/RHEL Arch openSUSE apt autoremove + apt clean Works Fails Fails Fails journalctl --vacuum-size=100M Works Works Works Works Disabled snap revisions Works If snap installed If snap installed If snap installed Kernel listing (dpkg --list) Works Silent — prints nothing Silent Silent /tmp files older than 7 days Works Works Works Works Page-cache drop Works Works Works Works The journal, /tmp and page-cache steps rely on journalctl, find and sysctl, which behave the same everywhere systemd is present. The kernel step is listing-only regardless, so its failure on non-dpkg systems costs nothing.

On a non-Debian system, run --system for the steps that work and handle packages natively: # Fedora / RHEL / Rocky sudo dnf autoremove sudo dnf clean all # Arch / Manjaro (paccache is in pacman-contrib) sudo pacman -Rns "$(pacman -Qtdq)" # orphans, if any sudo paccache -r # keep the last 3 versions sudo pacman -Scc # clear the whole package cache # openSUSE sudo zypper clean --all sudo zypper packages --orphaned Then let linux-cleanup do the rest, which is where most of the space is anyway: linux-cleanup --all-safe -y

Every $HOME cache category is distro-independent, because the paths come from the tools themselves rather than the distribution: Package-manager caches — yarn, npm, pnpm, pip, composer, bun, deno Browser caches — Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Chromium, Edge, Vivaldi Build-tool caches — Gradle, Cypress, Playwright, TypeScript Developer-tool data — Android AVDs, Flutter pub-cache, Dart, flatpak Editor extensions — VS Code, Cursor node_modules, partial downloads, personal stale files All read-only modes, every safety guard, session records and logs

Alpine and other minimal images typically ship BusyBox rather than GNU coreutils. The tool needs GNU find, du, stat and especially realpath — the last is what resolves symlinks before the protected-path check. apk add coreutils findutils bash linux-cleanup --self-test --self-test names the first missing dependency. Do not run destructive modes until it passes.

Works normally. linux-cleanup runs on the Linux side and behaves exactly as it would on bare metal. It does not walk into /mnt/c/. If you have symlinked ~/Downloads to a Windows directory, the allowlist resolves the symlink before deciding, so Windows-side Documents and Pictures are refused the same as native ones.
Not supported. The npm package declares "os": ["linux"] and will refuse to install. Paths, find flags and package managers all differ.

Symptom-specific problems belong in Troubleshooting; design rationale is in Safety guards.

Your source files, no. ~/Documents and the other personal directories are protected outright, and no cleanup target points at a project's source. The closest it comes is finding stale node_modules directories inside your project roots. Those are interactive-only with per-project confirmation, and yarn install rebuilds them. One caveat worth knowing: if you edited a file inside node_modules directly, rather than through a patch tool, that edit exists nowhere else.

No. Zero network calls. No telemetry, no analytics, no crash upload, no update check. Verify it yourself on a clone: grep -rE 'curl|wget|http://|https://' cleanup.sh lib/ modules/ bin/ Matches appear only in the version banner's URLs, the mailto: feedback helper, and comments. There is no network code path. The only data that leaves your machine is what you choose to email.

An undo log would be write amplification on the disk you are trying to free — keeping 20 GB in order to reclaim 20 GB accomplishes nothing. It would also create false confidence, and be partial at best. The safety model is prevention instead: an allowlist, a staleness gate, and interactive confirmation. Full reasoning: Deletion is permanent.
No. Read-only inspection is a separate mode, --scan. Passing --dry-run exits with code 2 for an unknown flag — do not treat that as a safety net. See Preview before deleting.

linux-cleanup --self-test # verifies the guards actually fire linux-cleanup --scan # read-only; shows what would be reclaimed linux-cleanup --list-targets # every path it can touch After those three you have seen the safety model work without losing a byte. Then run linux-cleanup and answer n to anything that surprises you.
documents.s: What is the safest way to try it?

documents.t: A little, sometimes, and it is worth being honest about how little: VS Code launches faster with a dozen extension directories rather than fifty A cold cache is marginally faster to skim than a bloated one Browser cold-starts are unaffected — caches are key-value, lookups are O(1) The page-cache drop frees RAM, not disk, and the kernel refills it immediately The real benefit is that "disk full" stops blocking your work — not a benchmark number.
documents.s: Will it speed up my computer?

documents.t: The current removal finishes — usually well under a second — then the script exits with code 130. The log keeps everything up to that point. The crash trap deliberately ignores 130, so no crash bundle is written.
documents.s: What if I press Ctrl-C mid-cleanup?

documents.t: You can, but you should not. It is designed to run as a normal user, and running as root only widens the blast radius if a bug ever slipped past the guards. --system handles the legitimate sudo needs internally, one audited command at a time.

Bash is already on every system this targets. A compiled binary would mean shipping something users cannot easily audit; a Python or Node implementation would add a runtime dependency to a tool whose entire job is removing things from your disk. The script is a few thousand lines of commented bash that a senior engineer can read in an afternoon. For a tool that runs rm -rf with sudo available, auditability is worth more than ergonomics.

documents.t: It disables the staleness gate, wiping caches in full rather than pruning idle files. That includes Gradle wrapper distributions, Playwright browsers and Cypress binaries you might still want. It is the right choice before reimaging a machine and a poor default otherwise. Never combine it with a cron job.

linux-cleanup ships three ways: npx with no install, a global npm install, or a git clone. All three run the same Bash script — the npm package is a thin Node launcher that locates cleanup.sh and points logs and reports at a persistent directory. Version note The npm registry reported 1.6.0 on 2026-10-14. Versions 1.5.0–1.6.0 include safety fixes; they are not behaviorally identical to 1.4.0. See the changelog before upgrading an older install.

The fastest way to evaluate it. Nothing lands on your PATH and nothing is left behind if you decide against it. npx linux-cleanup --version npx linux-cleanup --scan # read-only audit npx linux-cleanup # guided walkthrough npx fetches the package into a temporary npm cache directory. Your logs and reports are written to ~/.linux-cleanup/ — not the temp directory — so they survive npm cache eviction and are still there next time.

npm install -g linux-cleanup linux-cleanup --version linux-cleanup is then on your PATH everywhere. Logs and reports still go to ~/.linux-cleanup/. npm install -g linux-cleanup@latest # upgrade npm uninstall -g linux-cleanup # remove Uninstalling the package does not remove a shell alias or cron entry you installed — see Uninstall for the complete removal.

For reading the source, auditing it, or modifying it. The repository contents are what npm publishes. git clone https://github.com/aoneahsan/linux-cleanup ~/linux-cleanup cd ~/linux-cleanup chmod +x cleanup.sh ./cleanup.sh --self-test ./cleanup.sh The one behavioural difference: a clone keeps its output alongside the source, in <clone>/logs/, <clone>/reports/ and <clone>/feedback/, rather than in ~/.linux-cleanup/. Both are overridable with LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME. See Output paths. The project is MIT licensed, so forks and modifications are fine.

linux-cleanup --version # confirms which build you actually have linux-cleanup --self-test # dependency, syntax and safety-guard checks A clean self-test ends with a pass message. It asserts that the protected-path guard really does refuse /, $HOME, ~/Documents, ~/.ssh and /etc, and that it does not refuse ~/.cache/yarn. Any failed assertion exits non-zero. Run --self-test after every upgrade It is the only check that runs against the code you actually have rather than against documentation. It takes a second.
documents.s: Verify before you run anything destructive

documents.t: If you… Use Want to try it once npx Will run it regularly, or from cron Global npm install Want to read or modify the source git clone Are on a machine without Node.js git clone Need output kept next to the source git clone For cron specifically, prefer a global install and use an absolute path in the crontab — cron runs with a minimal PATH and will not find a ~/.local/bin install. This is the single most common cron problem; see Alias and cron.

No system service, no background daemon, no scheduled task (until you ask for one) No telemetry agent, no update checker, no remote configuration fetch No shell configuration changes unless you run --install-alias or --doctor No files outside the package and ~/.linux-cleanup/, and the latter only once you actually run it

A first session takes about ten minutes and typically reclaims 5–30 GB on a developer machine. This page walks it end to end: verify, preview, run guided, read the report. Do not skip steps 1 and 2 They take two minutes and they are the difference between a cleanup you controlled and one you discovered afterwards. This tool deletes permanently.

npx linux-cleanup --version npx linux-cleanup --self-test --version confirms which build you have. --self-test checks dependencies, shell syntax, and asserts the safety guards actually fire. A clean run ends with a pass message; any failed assertion exits non-zero and you should stop there.

npx linux-cleanup --scan --scan is read-only. It walks every category, measures real sizes, prints what could be reclaimed, and writes a JSON report. Nothing is deleted. Read the output before continuing. Common findings on a developer laptop: Category Typical size ~/.cache/yarn + ~/.npm + pnpm store 5–25 GB Chrome / Brave / Firefox profile caches 2–8 GB ~/.gradle/caches 3–10 GB Cypress + Playwright browser binaries 1–4 GB ~/.android/avd (emulator images) 6–30 GB Stale node_modules in old projects 5–50 GB Two things to look for specifically: any path you did not expect (a symlinked cache, for instance), and any personal-file candidate — those are the only entries that can be irreplaceable.

npx linux-cleanup No flags means the guided walkthrough: ten steps, each asking before it does anything, with a running total of bytes reclaimed. At each step you get three choices: Key Effect a Run this step (the default — pressing Enter chooses it) s Skip this step q Quit the walkthrough now Inside a step, individual targets get their own [Y/n] confirmation. So there are two levels: skip a whole category, or accept the category and decline specific items. The ten steps, in order: Package-manager caches Application caches Developer-tool data Editor old extensions Stale node_modules Partial / orphan downloads Personal stale files System cleanup (sudo) Final size audit Generate readable report Steps 6 and 7 are the ones to slow down on Everything before them is regenerable. Partial downloads and personal stale files are not — read each candidate rather than accepting the batch. Skip both with s on a first run if you would rather review them separately later. Aborting with Ctrl-C is safe at any point. The current removal finishes, the script exits with code 130, and partial progress is preserved in the log.

The session ends with a summary naming the log and report files: ✓ Recovered: 18.7 GB ℹ Log saved: ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-2026-05-10_140312.log ℹ Report: ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-2026-05-10_140312.json The JSON report is canonical and always written. To convert it for reading or archiving — this needs jq: linux-cleanup --export both latest # Markdown + HTML beside the JSON linux-cleanup --reports # interactive reports manager See Reports.

Only after a manual run you were happy with: linux-cleanup --install-alias # type `cleanup` from anywhere linux-cleanup --install-cron # weekly --all-safe -y, Sundays at 03:00 The cron job runs --all-safe -y, which auto-confirms regenerable caches only. It cannot touch personal files — --yes is ignored by those modes. See Alias and cron for exactly what each writes and how to remove it.

These are present on essentially every mainstream distro. bash, find, du, df, rm, awk, sort, grep, sed, stat, realpath. realpath matters more than the others: it is what resolves symlinks before the protected-path check. On a minimal container image without GNU coreutils, install them before running. npx linux-cleanup --self-test --self-test probes every required command and names the first one missing, with a fix hint. Each unlocks one feature. Without it, that feature is unavailable and the rest of the tool is unaffected. Dependency Unlocks Without it jq Markdown / HTML report export JSON reports still written; conversion unavailable whiptail The visual TUI menu --tui falls back to the CLI menu with an install hint dialog TUI fallback when whiptail is absent As above snap Disabled snap-revision cleanup in --system That step is skipped cleanly crontab The weekly cron installer --install-cron cannot run numfmt Human-readable byte sizes Falls back to raw byte counts xdg-open Opening HTML reports in a browser Open the file manually less Paged JSON view in the reports manager Read the file directly lsb_release Better distro detection in feedback bundles Bundle still generated

jq (report export) and whiptail (visual menu) are the two most people want. # Debian / Ubuntu / Mint sudo apt install jq whiptail # Fedora / RHEL / Rocky sudo dnf install jq newt # Arch / Manjaro sudo pacman -S jq libnewt # openSUSE sudo zypper install jq newt The whiptail binary ships in the newt package on RPM-based distros and libnewt on Arch.

Cache cleanup inside $HOME — which is the large majority of what this tool reclaims — works identically on every Linux distribution. --system is Debian/Ubuntu only The sudo mode calls apt and dpkg directly, with no distro detection and no guard. On Fedora, Arch or openSUSE its package steps fail with "command not found". Full breakdown of which steps work where: Distro support.

The tool's own output is negligible: a session log is 50–500 KB, a JSON report 5–50 KB, a feedback bundle 50–200 KB. A year of weekly cron runs totals a few megabytes. See Output paths for the layout and how to thin old files.
Installation — the three install paths Quick start — your first cleanup
Two one-time setup helpers: a cleanup shell alias, and a weekly automated run. Both are reversible with a matching uninstall flag. linux-cleanup --install-alias linux-cleanup --install-cron

linux-cleanup --install-alias Appends a cleanup alias to ~/.bash_aliases or ~/.zshrc, depending on your shell. Afterwards, typing cleanup anywhere runs the tool. Reload your shell or the alias will not appear to exist: source ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc Remove it with linux-cleanup --uninstall-alias. Shell-init files are protected at the deletion layer .bashrc, .zshrc, .bash_aliases and similar are on the protected-basename list, so no cleanup mode can ever delete one — regardless of the path it appears at. The alias installer appends; the uninstaller removes only its own line.
linux-cleanup --install-cron Schedules --all-safe -y for Sundays at 03:00, appending output to ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log. Requires crontab. Remove it with linux-cleanup --uninstall-cron.

It is the only mode --yes applies to, and it cannot touch personal data — the interactive-only modes are not part of it and ignore --yes by design. So an unattended run can clear caches and can never delete a file from ~/Downloads. See Guard 3. The staleness gate still applies, so recently-used files survive each weekly pass.
documents.s: Why --all-safe is the right mode for this

documents.t: For a different schedule or flags: crontab -e 0 3 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --no-report --cleanup-logs >>~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log 2>&1 Use an absolute path Cron runs with a minimal PATH — typically just /usr/bin:/bin. A bare linux-cleanup will not be found if it lives in ~/.local/bin or a Node version-manager directory, and the job fails silently every week. This is the most common problem with scheduled runs. Find your path with: command -v linux-cleanup Or set PATH= explicitly at the top of the crontab. Flag Why in cron --all-safe -y Unattended, caches only --no-report Stops JSON records accumulating — they are never auto-deleted --cleanup-logs Removes that run's log at the end -d 30 Optional: more aggressive weekly pruning --cleanup-logs alone is not enough to keep the directory small: it never touches records. --no-report is the flag that does. Do not add --purge-all to a scheduled job Unattended plus no staleness gate means an expensive asset can disappear the week before you need it, with nobody watching. Keep --purge-all for deliberate, supervised runs. See Reclaim the most space.

tail -100 ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log crontab -l | grep -i cleanup If the log shows command not found, it is the PATH problem above. If the log is empty, the job never fired — check that the cron daemon is running (systemctl status cron or crond). The cron log is never rotated. Rotate it yourself when it grows: mv ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log.old touch ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log

If you prefer timers to cron, there is nothing tool-specific about it — schedule the same command. The tool neither knows nor cares which scheduler invoked it, and --install-cron is a convenience rather than a requirement.
linux-cleanup --uninstall-alias linux-cleanup --uninstall-cron Full removal including the package itself: Uninstall.
An ordered recipe, safest first. Each stage reclaims more than the last and carries slightly more trade-off. Stop wherever you have enough space.

linux-cleanup --audit # 20 largest entries in $HOME linux-cleanup --scan # what this tool can reclaim Do this first. If a 60 GB VM image or a Steam library is the real problem, no amount of cache cleaning will help and you will have spent an hour finding that out the slow way. --audit shows everything; --scan shows only what the tool can address. See Home audit.
documents.s: Stage 0 — Find out what is actually using the disk

documents.t: linux-cleanup --all-safe -y Every regenerable cache, pruned at the 100-day default. Typically 5–25 GB. Cannot touch personal files. This is the stage that reclaims the most per unit of risk, and the one to schedule weekly.

linux-cleanup --node-modules -d 90 Frequently the biggest single win on a developer machine: 5–50 GB. Interactive, so you confirm each project. Anything you have not opened in three months is a safe candidate — yarn install rebuilds it. Two things to watch for: a dependency you patched in place, and a project with no committed lockfile. See node_modules finder.

linux-cleanup --system apt cache, journal, snap revisions, /tmp. Typically 2–8 GB on a machine that has been running a year. Debian and Ubuntu only On other distros the apt steps fail and you should run your package manager's equivalent by hand. See Distro support.

linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -d 30 Drops the staleness gate from 100 days to 30, so more of each cache qualifies. Adds maybe 2–10 GB on top of stage 1. The trade-off is real but modest: something you used six weeks ago gets re-fetched next time you need it.

linux-cleanup --stale -d 365 # start here linux-cleanup --stale -d 180 # then, if you need more Large idle files in ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop. Can be 1–50 GB, entirely depending on your habits. This is the only stage that can destroy something irreplaceable Read every candidate. Starting at 365 days gives a short, obvious list; work down from there rather than starting aggressive. See Stale personal files and Deletion is permanent.

linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --purge-all Disables the staleness gate entirely. Every cache target is wiped whole. Adds 3–15 GB beyond stage 4. What this specifically costs you The gate exists to protect assets that look like cache but are expensive to replace: Gradle wrapper distributions — ~230 MB each, re-downloaded on the next build with that wrapper Playwright and Cypress browser binaries — re-downloaded on the next test run Yarn-cached tarballs of pinned dependencies None is irreplaceable; all cost bandwidth and a slow first run afterwards. This is a reasonable choice before reimaging a machine, and a poor default.

Cumulative, on a developer laptop with a year of accumulation: Through stage Typical reclaim 1 — safe batch 5–25 GB 2 — node_modules 10–75 GB 3 — system 12–83 GB 4 — 30-day threshold 14–93 GB 5 — personal files 15–140 GB 6 — full purge 18–155 GB Ranges are wide because machines differ enormously. Your --scan output is the honest estimate; these are only a shape.

If you still need space, the tool cannot help with these — but knowing that is progress: VM images and container storage Game libraries Datasets and model weights Anything in ~/Documents, ~/Pictures, ~/Music, ~/Videos — all protected and never candidates --audit from stage 0 shows them, and du -sh ~/* | sort -rh | head narrows further.

linux-cleanup --install-cron # weekly --all-safe -y, Sundays 03:00 Stage 1 running automatically stops most of the accumulation. Stages 2, 3 and 5 stay manual — they need your judgement. See Alias and cron.

Two commands produce everything a maintainer needs. Nothing is transmitted automatically — you review the bundle and send it yourself. linux-cleanup --debug-bundle # package the latest log + session record linux-cleanup --feedback # instructions, and an optional mailto draft

linux-cleanup --debug-bundle Writes ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-<timestamp>.tar.gz containing: The latest session log The latest JSON session record, if one exists A MANIFEST.txt with distro, kernel, bash version and self-test output Then: linux-cleanup --feedback Prints what to include and offers to open a pre-filled mailto: draft with system information already completed.

A bundle contains paths from your machine Not file contents — but the log names every path touched, which means directory names, project names, and sometimes filenames from ~/Downloads. Inspect it first: tar -tzf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-*.tar.gz # list contents tar -xzOf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-*.tar.gz # read it in full If something in there is sensitive, extract the bundle, remove or redact the file, and re-archive — or just send the manifest plus the specific lines that matter.
documents.s: Review the bundle before sending it

documents.t: Since 1.3.0, an unexpected non-zero exit writes crash-<timestamp>.tar.gz to the same directory automatically, and prints the path. It holds the active log, the most recent record, and a system manifest including the exit code. Nothing is sent. The tool has no network code path — see Privacy. The bundle sits on your disk until you decide. Crash bundles are not written for expected exits: 0, 130 (Ctrl-C), 143 (SIGTERM) and 2 (argument error) are all excluded. See Exit codes.

A good report is short and specific: Include Example Distro and version lsb_release -d Bash version bash --version | head -1 Tool version linux-cleanup --version The exact command linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -d 30 Expected versus actual "expected the Gradle wrapper kept, it was deleted" The bundle Attach the tar.gz The most valuable line is expected versus actual. A log alone shows what happened but not why you think it was wrong.

Route Use for GitHub issues Bugs, feature requests — preferred, public aoneahsan@gmail.com Anything you would rather not post publicly A pull request You have a fix. MIT licensed, forks welcome Feature requests by description are as welcome as code. Say what you would want cleaned and why the existing modes do not cover it.

Anything contradicting the documented safety model: A deletion inside a protected path A current editor extension version removed, not just a superseded one A file deleted despite being newer than --days, without --purge-all A personal-data mode acting without confirmation Any network connection made by the tool Each of those is a safety-model violation rather than an inconvenience.

Nothing, unless you send it linux-cleanup makes zero network calls. No telemetry, no analytics, no crash upload, no update check. Verify on a clone: grep -rE 'curl|wget|http://|https://' cleanup.sh lib/ modules/ bin/ The only matches are the author's URLs in the version banner, the mailto: helper, and comments. There is no network code path. Logs, records and bundles are local files. The maintainer cannot see them, and cannot push a fix to your machine — a new version reaches you when you re-run npx or upgrade.
Troubleshooting — check here first Recovery — if data was lost Exit codes
Remove the automation first, then the package, then the data. Uninstalling the package does not remove a shell alias or cron entry you installed — those are separate.

linux-cleanup --uninstall-alias linux-cleanup --uninstall-cron Do this before removing the package, while the command still exists. If you have already removed it, see manual removal below. Verify: crontab -l | grep -i cleanup # expect no output grep -rn 'cleanup' ~/.bash_aliases ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null

npm uninstall -g linux-cleanup For npx, nothing is installed — the npm cache evicts it on its own. To clear it now: npm cache clean --force For a git clone, delete the directory: rm -rf ~/linux-cleanup A clone holds its own logs and records Unlike the npm install paths, a clone keeps output in <clone>/logs/ and <clone>/reports/. Deleting the clone deletes those too. Copy anything you want to keep first. See Output paths.

Logs, session records and feedback bundles live in ~/.linux-cleanup/ and are never removed by uninstalling. ls -la ~/.linux-cleanup/ # look before deleting rm -rf ~/.linux-cleanup/ They are small — usually a few megabytes — and they are the only account of what past runs deleted. Keeping them costs nothing; removing them is irreversible like anything else. If you set LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME, remove that directory instead, and drop the export from your shell configuration.
rm -f ~/.config/personal-roots.txt ~/.config/project-roots.txt Only present if you created them. See Environment variables.
documents.s: 4. Remove configuration, if you created any

documents.t: Undo both helpers by hand. Cron: crontab -e # delete the line containing linux-cleanup or cleanup.sh Alias: grep -n 'cleanup' ~/.bash_aliases ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null Remove the matching alias line with your editor, then source the file or open a new terminal.
documents.s: If you removed the package first

documents.t: Nothing, once the above is done. The tool installs no system service, no daemon, no systemd unit, no /etc entry and no root-owned file. Everything it creates is inside your home directory. Effects on your system it does not undo — because they are not files it owns: Deleted caches stay deleted. They regenerate as each tool needs them Shell-init blocks added by --doctor stay. They are the correct configuration for runtimes you have installed; remove them by hand if you want them gone
command -v linux-cleanup # expect no output crontab -l | grep -i cleanup # expect no output ls ~/.linux-cleanup 2>&1 # expect: No such file or directory
Installation — if you are reinstalling

--all-safe cleans every regenerable cache in a single pass. It is the mode for unattended maintenance and the only mode --yes applies to. linux-cleanup --all-safe # prompts per target linux-cleanup --all-safe -y # no prompts — the cron form

Safe means regenerable: package-manager caches, browser and application caches, and stale developer-tool data. It does not mean risk-free, and it does not mean reversible — deletions are still permanent. What --all-safe will never touch, regardless of --yes: Personal files in ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop or anywhere else Partial downloads node_modules directories Anything on the protected-path list Globally installed packages or shell-init files Those categories are interactive-only by design and are simply not part of this mode. This is what makes --all-safe -y acceptable in a cron job. Since 1.1.0 the mode also runs a startup assertion that aborts with a BUG: message if any protected runtime directory ever leaks into its target list, so a future regression fails loudly rather than deleting something it should not.

-y / --yes auto-confirms cache deletions. It is only valid with --all-safe; the interactive modes ignore it by policy. linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -y means you will not see the decisions until afterwards Everything is still gated by the allowlist and the staleness gate, and the log and report record every path touched — but you read them after the fact. For a first run, drop the -y and answer the prompts, or run --scan first.

By default --all-safe prunes each target rather than wiping it: only files whose atime and mtime are both older than --days (default 100) are removed. The summary reports bytes freed and bytes kept per target, so you can see what survived. linux-cleanup --all-safe -y # 100-day threshold linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -d 30 # more aggressive linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --purge-all # gate off — full wipe --purge-all in a cron job is a poor combination Unattended plus no staleness gate means a Gradle wrapper distribution or Playwright browser bundle can disappear the week before you need it, with nobody watching. Keep --purge-all for deliberate, before-reimaging runs.

linux-cleanup --install-cron This schedules --all-safe -y for Sundays at 03:00 and appends output to ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log. See Alias and cron for the exact entry and how to remove it. If you write the crontab entry yourself, use an absolute path — cron's minimal PATH will not find a ~/.local/bin install: 0 3 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --no-report --cleanup-logs >>~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log 2>&1 --no-report and --cleanup-logs keep an unattended job from accumulating files. Note that --cleanup-logs only removes that run's log; reports are never auto-deleted, which is why --no-report is the flag that actually keeps the directory small.

tail -100 ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log jq '.totals' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | tail -20 If the cron log shows command not found, the crontab is using a bare command name — see Troubleshooting.

--doctor finds runtimes that exist on disk but are not wired into your shell configuration, and offers to add the missing init block. Added in 1.1.0. linux-cleanup --doctor This is the mode for pnpm: command not found when you know perfectly well you installed pnpm.

Doctor never deletes or edits an existing line It appends a canonical init block, and only after you confirm. It does not modify, reorder, or remove anything already in your shell configuration. Shell-init files are additionally protected at the deletion layer: safe_rm refuses any path whose basename is .bashrc, .zshrc, .profile, .bash_aliases or similar, wherever it lives. See Protected paths.

Runtime Detects Appends nvm ~/.nvm present, no NVM_DIR init The standard nvm loader block pnpm ~/.local/share/pnpm present, not on PATH PNPM_HOME export and PATH addition bun ~/.bun present, not on PATH Bun's init block deno ~/.deno present, not on PATH Deno's PATH addition cargo ~/.cargo present, not on PATH . "$HOME/.cargo/env"

An installer writes its init block to a file your shell does not read. ~/.profile is only read by login shells; ~/.bash_profile shadows it when present; a change to ~/.bashrc never reaches a zsh session. The runtime installs fine and then appears to vanish. It also happens after migrating a dotfiles repository between machines, or after switching login shells.
Reload your shell, or the change will not appear to have worked: source ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc Then confirm: command -v pnpm && pnpm --version
--globals works even when a package manager is missing from PATH, by falling back to filesystem inspection. So if the audit lists pnpm globals but pnpm itself is not found, --doctor is the fix.
documents.s: Its relationship to the globals audit

documents.t: Globals audit Troubleshooting

--editor-ext removes superseded VS Code and Cursor extension versions. When an extension updates, the old version directory often stays on disk. On a machine with many extensions and a few years of updates this accumulates to hundreds of megabytes. linux-cleanup --editor-ext

A version directory is a candidate only when both hold: A newer version of the same extension exists — the current version is never a candidate That older version has been idle for --days or more (default 100) The second condition was added in 1.2.1. Before that, supersession alone was enough, which removed old versions you had loaded recently. Output shows per-version idle days, so you can see why something was kept.
The current version of any extension Extension settings, keybindings, or workspace state Anything in ~/.config — that whole tree is protected Extensions in an editor other than VS Code and Cursor

If VS Code shows a missing-extension banner, reload the window: Ctrl+Shift+P → Developer: Reload Window. The editor is holding a reference to a directory that no longer exists. If an extension is genuinely gone — which would mean the "highest version" detection mis-identified the current one — reinstall it and please report the bug: code --install-extension <publisher>.<name>
Typically 100 MB to 1 GB. Modest next to caches, but it also trims editor startup: VS Code scans the extensions directory at launch, so fewer directories means a marginally faster start.
Runs as step 4 of the guided walkthrough, and is included in --all-safe since it only ever removes regenerable, superseded copies.
The staleness gate Modes overview

--globals lists your globally installed packages across npm, pnpm, yarn, bun and deno, and marks each one. Added in 1.1.0. linux-cleanup --globals linux-cleanup --globals -d 180 This mode never deletes anything It prints copy-pasteable uninstall commands and stops. You decide what to run. Global packages are exactly the kind of thing that breaks a workflow when removed by surprise, so the tool refuses to remove them for you.

Verdict Meaning recently used Modified or accessed within --days. Leave it needed by: <pkg> Another global declares it as a dependency. Removing it breaks that one STALE — safe to uninstall Idle past the threshold and nothing else depends on it "Safe to uninstall" means safe from the perspective of the other globals on your machine. It cannot know about a shell script, a CI job, or a habit of yours that calls the binary. Read the list before acting.

Globally installed packages are never deleted by any cleanup mode. ~/.local/share/pnpm, ~/.npm, ~/.yarn, ~/.bun/install/global and ~/.deno/bin are on the exact-match protected list specifically to keep them safe — a lesson from a real bug where the pnpm cleanup targeted the install root and wiped global packages. See 1.1.0. This audit is the deliberate counterpart: visibility without automation.

Each manager is queried through its CLI when available, and through filesystem inspection when not. So the audit still works on a machine where pnpm was installed but is not currently on PATH — which is often exactly the situation you are trying to diagnose. If a runtime is on disk but not wired into your shell, --doctor is the mode that fixes that.
documents.s: Works without the package managers on PATH

documents.t: Before reinstalling Node or switching version managers Before migrating to a new machine — it is a portable inventory of your tooling When npm ls -g output has become unrecognisable Once or twice a year, as hygiene
Doctor — repair a runtime that is installed but not on PATH Protected paths — why globals are never touched
--audit lists the 20 largest entries in $HOME, sorted by size. It deletes nothing and it does not care whether the tool can clean what it finds. linux-cleanup --audit

--scan measures the categories linux-cleanup knows how to clean. --audit measures your home directory, full stop. That difference is the point. If a 60 GB VM image, a downloaded dataset, or a Steam library is what actually filled your disk, --scan will never mention it and --audit will put it at the top of the list. --audit --scan Scope Everything in $HOME Only cleanable categories Answers What is using my disk? What can this tool reclaim? Writes a report No Yes Deletes Never Never

linux-cleanup --audit # what is big? linux-cleanup --scan # what can this tool reclaim? If the audit's top entries appear in the scan, the tool can help. If they do not, you have learned something more useful — the space is somewhere this tool does not go, and you can deal with it directly. Common large things linux-cleanup will not clean: VM images and container storage (~/.local/share/libvirt, ~/.local/share/docker) Game libraries (Steam, Lutris) Datasets, model weights, media libraries Anything in ~/Documents, ~/Pictures, ~/Music, ~/Videos — all protected
du -sh ~/.local/share/* | sort -rh | head -20 du -sh ~/* | sort -rh | head -20 --audit is the fast first pass; du narrows it down once you know where to look.
Scan — what the tool can reclaim Reclaim the most space
--menu prints a numbered list of every category and runs the one you pick. Use it when you know what you want and do not need the ten-step tour. linux-cleanup --menu # or: -m, -i, --interactive

Menu Walkthrough Order You choose Fixed, ten steps Scope One category per selection Everything, in sequence Loops Returns to the menu afterwards Runs to the end Report Per action One session report Best for Targeted cleanup First runs, full sweeps The safety model is identical. Every category behaves exactly as it does in the walkthrough — the allowlist, the staleness gate and per-target confirmation all apply. Picking a personal-data category from the menu still gives you per-entry prompts, and --yes still has no effect on it.
documents.s: How it differs from the walkthrough

documents.t: linux-cleanup --menu -d 30 # 30-day threshold for whatever you pick linux-cleanup --menu --purge-all # staleness gate off linux-cleanup --menu --no-color # plain output

--tui is the same menu rendered as a whiptail or dialog box. It needs one of those installed; --menu needs nothing beyond bash and works over any connection, including a dumb terminal or a ssh -T session where a full-screen dialog would misbehave.

--node-modules finds node_modules directories in projects you have not touched for --days or more, and offers each for deletion. On a machine with years of side projects this is frequently the biggest single reclaim available — 5 to 50 GB. linux-cleanup --node-modules # 100-day default linux-cleanup --node-modules -d 90
This mode requires per-project confirmation and ignores --yes. It is not part of --all-safe and cannot be run unattended. See Guard 3.

It scans your project roots for node_modules directories whose containing project has been idle past the threshold, and reports each with its size and idle days. Nested node_modules inside an already-listed directory are not counted separately. Project roots are configurable via project-roots.txt under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default ~/.config). See Environment variables.

node_modules is the most reliably regenerable thing on a developer machine — yarn install or npm install rebuilds it from the lockfile. Two caveats worth knowing before you accept everything: Two ways this can still cost you A patched dependency. If you edited a file inside node_modules directly rather than through patch-package or a yarn patch, that edit exists nowhere else. It is not in any registry and not in your lockfile. No lockfile, no network. Reinstalling needs the registry to be reachable and the lockfile to be present. A project with no committed lockfile may not resolve to the same dependency tree — and an air-gapped machine may not resolve at all. Neither is common, and neither is detectable by the tool. If either applies to a project in the list, decline that one.
The project source — only the node_modules directory inside it Lockfiles, package.json, or anything else in the project Projects touched within the threshold Anything on the protected-path list

linux-cleanup --node-modules -d 30 Lowering the threshold widens the candidate list. At 30 days you will start seeing projects you are still occasionally working on, so read the list rather than accepting in bulk — the cost of a mistake is a reinstall, which is minor but not free.
This runs as step 5 of the guided walkthrough, with the same per-project prompts.
Reclaim the most space Safety guards

linux-cleanup has one entry point and picks its mode from a single flag. Running it with no flag gives you the guided walkthrough. Modes are mutually exclusive — pass one. Options like --days and --yes combine with them.

Safe to run at any time, on any machine, without thinking about it. Mode Flag Shows Scan -s --scan Every cache category with current sizes Home audit --audit The 20 largest entries in $HOME Globals audit --globals Global npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/deno packages List targets --list-targets Every path the tool can touch, plus the protected list Self-test --self-test Dependency, syntax and safety-guard checks Version -V --version Version and author

These delete, and every one of them asks first unless you pass --yes. Mode Flag Behaviour Walkthrough (default) -w Ten guided steps, prompt before each Menu -m --menu Numbered menu — pick one category TUI -t --tui The same, as a whiptail/dialog dialog All-safe -a --all-safe Every regenerable cache in one pass Editor extensions --editor-ext Superseded VS Code / Cursor versions System cleanup --system apt, journal, snap, /tmp, page cache — needs sudo

Personal or project data. These ignore --yes and require per-entry confirmation. See Guard 3. Mode Flag Finds Stale personal files -p --stale Large idle files in ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop Partial downloads --partials .fdmdownload, .crdownload, .part node_modules finder --node-modules Project dependency dirs idle N+ days

Mode Flag Purpose Reports --reports List, convert, view past session reports Export --export FMT ID Non-interactive conversion Doctor --doctor Repair broken shell-init for nvm, pnpm, bun, deno, cargo Feedback --feedback Bug-report instructions, optional mailto draft Debug bundle --debug-bundle Package latest log + report into a tar.gz Install alias --install-alias Add a cleanup shell alias Install cron --install-cron Weekly --all-safe -y, Sundays 03:00 Uninstall alias / cron --uninstall-alias --uninstall-cron Remove either

Goal Mode First time using the tool --self-test, then --scan, then no flag Free space now, with control (default walkthrough) Free space now, no prompts --all-safe -y One specific category --menu or --tui Weekly unattended maintenance --all-safe -y via --install-cron Maximum reclaim before reimaging --all-safe -y --purge-all Find what is eating the disk --audit then --scan Old side projects piling up --node-modules command not found after install --doctor

Option Default Effect -d N --days N 100 Staleness threshold. Lower is more aggressive --purge-all off Disables the staleness gate — full wipe -y --yes off Auto-confirm regenerable caches. Only with --all-safe --no-report off Skip the JSON report. Logs still written --cleanup-logs off Delete this run's log at the end. Reports always kept --no-color off Disable ANSI colour. NO_COLOR also honoured Full detail: CLI flags and the modes matrix.

--partials finds abandoned partial-download files and offers them for deletion. These are the placeholder files a browser or download manager writes while transferring, and forgets to clean up when the transfer is interrupted. linux-cleanup --partials

Extension Written by .crdownload Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Edge, Vivaldi .part Firefox, wget, aria2 .fdmdownload Free Download Manager A partial file holds however many bytes arrived before the transfer died — sometimes a few kilobytes, sometimes most of a multi-gigabyte ISO.
Per-file confirmation, --yes ignored, not part of --all-safe. See Guard 3.

A partial file may still be resumable — but usually is not Resuming needs the original download session: the browser's download-manager entry, the source URL, and a server that supports range requests. If the browser has been restarted or the download entry cleared, the partial is unresumable and is pure waste. The file itself is never independently useful — a half-downloaded archive does not open. So the practical question is only whether you still intend to resume it. Check before accepting a large one: Open your browser's downloads page and look for a paused or failed entry matching the filename If there is one, resume it there rather than deleting the partial If there is not, the partial is orphaned and safe to remove

A download running right now also has a .crdownload or .part file. The tool has no way to distinguish an in-progress transfer from an abandoned one. Deleting an active partial breaks the transfer in progress — so check your downloads page if you are unsure, or run this mode when nothing is downloading.
documents.s: An active download will show up here

documents.t: Step 6 of the guided walkthrough.
Stale personal files — the related interactive mode Deletion is permanent

--stale finds files over about 10 MB in ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop that have been unused for --days or more, and offers them for deletion one at a time. linux-cleanup --stale # or: -p linux-cleanup --stale -d 180 # only files idle 180+ days This is the only mode that can delete something irreplaceable Every other category holds data some program can rebuild. ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop hold whatever you put there — including, sometimes, the only copy of something that matters. The tool cannot tell an installer you will never open again from a document you have not needed yet. It does not try. Read every candidate.

Per-file or per-range confirmation is mandatory. --yes is ignored here and always will be, and this mode is not part of --all-safe. See Guard 3. The candidate list is printed in full before anything is asked, so running the mode and declining everything is a legitimate way to audit those directories.

Three conditions together: It lives in a configured personal root — by default ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop It is larger than roughly 10 MB Both atime and mtime are older than --days (default 100) Personal roots are configurable through personal-roots.txt under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default ~/.config). See Environment variables. Why ~/Downloads is not on the protected list It cannot be — cleaning it is the entire point of this mode. The allowlist protects ~/Documents, ~/Pictures, ~/Music and ~/Videos precisely so that the one directory it does reach is the one you expect. If you keep things you care about in ~/Downloads, move them somewhere protected — that is the durable fix, and it protects them from more than this tool.
documents.s: What makes a file a candidate

documents.t: Each entry shows path, size and idle days. Worth pausing on: Pattern Consider Installers, ISOs, .deb/.AppImage Usually safe — re-downloadable Anything you produced rather than downloaded Keep, or move somewhere protected Client or work deliverables Keep. Downloads is a bad home for them Media with no obvious source Investigate before accepting Archives you never extracted Check the contents first

linux-cleanup --audit # what is actually large in $HOME linux-cleanup --stale -d 365 # only genuinely ancient files Starting at 365 days and working down gives you a short, obvious list first. Once that is clear, lower the threshold.
Step 7 of the guided walkthrough. Skipping it there with s and running it separately later — when you have time to read carefully — is a reasonable habit.
Deletion is permanent Partial downloads — the related interactive mode Home audit — find what is large first

Every session writes a canonical JSON session record to ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-<timestamp>.json. It is the durable account of what happened, and it is never auto-deleted. Markdown and HTML are optional conversions produced on demand. linux-cleanup --reports # interactive manager linux-cleanup --export both latest # non-interactive conversion

Section Holds schema_version Currently 1 credits Tool name, version, homepage, licence, author details meta Timestamps, duration, host, user, mode, staleness threshold, log path, launcher disk Filesystem usage before and after memory Memory usage before and after steps One entry per step: number, title, status, bytes freed totals Total bytes reclaimed, human-readable total, steps run and skipped Full field-by-field reference: Report schema.

linux-cleanup --reports Lists past sessions and lets you view one, convert it to Markdown or HTML, open the HTML in a browser, or delete it. Conversion options are hidden when jq is not installed — see below.

Non-interactive, for scripts and habits: linux-cleanup --export both latest # Markdown + HTML from the newest record linux-cleanup --export html all # every record to HTML linux-cleanup --export md 3 # record #3 to Markdown Argument Accepts Format md, html, both Identifier a record number, latest, or all Output lands beside the JSON with the same timestamp in the filename. The HTML is self-contained — embedded CSS, dark-mode aware, no external assets — so it can be emailed or archived as a single file.

JSON is always written; conversion is the optional part Without jq, the canonical JSON is still produced on every run. Only Markdown and HTML export are unavailable, and step 10 of the walkthrough records itself as skipped (jq missing). sudo apt install jq # Debian / Ubuntu sudo dnf install jq # Fedora / RHEL sudo pacman -S jq # Arch The generated HTML escapes every JSON-derived value through jq's @html filter, so a malformed input cannot inject markup into the rendered page.

The JSON is meant to be read by tools: # Total reclaimed by the most recent session jq '.totals.total_reclaimed_human' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | tail -1 # Every step that actually ran, most recent session jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran") | {title, freed_bytes}' \ "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" # Reclaim across every recorded session jq -s 'map(.totals.total_reclaimed_bytes) | add' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json

These records are never deleted automatically — not even by --cleanup-logs, which only removes the current run's log file. They are small, 5–50 KB each, so a year of weekly runs stays under a megabyte. To thin them yourself: find ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/ -name 'report-*' -mtime +90 -delete Skip generation entirely for a single run with --no-report; the log is still written.

A session record names what was deleted, not the data It holds paths and sizes. It contains none of the removed content, and nothing in it can restore anything. Its value after an unwanted deletion is telling you exactly what to restore from your own backup, or re-download. See Recovery.
Report schema — every field Output paths — where files land Recovery — using a session record after a surprise

--scan walks every cleanup category, measures what is there, and prints what could be reclaimed. It deletes nothing. This is the closest thing the tool has to a dry run, and it is the command to reach for first. linux-cleanup --scan # or: -s

For each category — package-manager caches, application caches, developer-tool data, editor extensions, node_modules, partial downloads, personal candidates — it stats the paths, sums the sizes, and prints a per-category breakdown with a total. It also writes a JSON report to ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/, so you have a timestamped record of what the disk looked like before you changed anything. --scan is safe to run: On a machine you have never run the tool on On someone else's machine From a cron job, purely to record a baseline While other work is in progress The only side effects are the log and the report.

Three things deserve attention. Unexpected paths. If a cache appears somewhere you did not expect, investigate before cleaning. The usual cause is a symlink. Resolve it yourself: realpath ~/.cache/yarn The allowlist resolves symlinks too and will refuse a target that lands inside a protected directory — but knowing about it beforehand is better than being surprised by a refusal message. Expensive categories. Gradle wrapper distributions, Cypress and Playwright binaries, and Android AVDs cost minutes and hundreds of megabytes to re-fetch. See What it deletes. Personal-file candidates. The only entries that can be irreplaceable. Read every one.

The reclaim figure is what exists at scan time, before the staleness gate is applied at deletion time. So the actual cleanup usually frees less than the scan suggested, because files touched within the threshold are kept. The gap between the two numbers is the gate protecting recently-used data — it is the tool working correctly, not an inconsistency. To see how much the gate is holding back, compare: linux-cleanup --scan # everything present linux-cleanup --scan -d 1 # what a 1-day threshold would consider stale

documents.t: The first scan on a large $HOME can take one to three minutes, dominated by find walking thousands of node_modules directories. Subsequent runs are faster because the kernel caches directory metadata. If it seems stuck, watch the log rather than the terminal: tail -f ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-*.log New lines every five to ten seconds means it is working. See Troubleshooting.

NO_COLOR=1 linux-cleanup --scan --no-report > /tmp/scan.log --no-report skips JSON generation when you only want the log. Exit code 0 means the scan completed; see Exit codes. To query a report programmatically, use the JSON rather than parsing terminal output: jq '.totals' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | tail -20

Mode Answers --scan What could be reclaimed here, right now --list-targets What paths could ever be touched --audit What is largest in $HOME, cleanable or not --globals Which global packages are unused --self-test Whether the safety guards work --audit is worth pairing with --scan: the scan only knows about categories the tool cleans, while the audit shows the largest things in your home directory whether or not this tool can help with them. A 60 GB VM image will show in the audit and never in the scan.

--system is the only mode that calls sudo. It runs six steps against system-managed storage, each prompting separately. linux-cleanup --system This mode is Debian/Ubuntu only The package steps call apt and dpkg directly. There is no distro detection and no command -v guard, so on Fedora, Arch or openSUSE those steps fail with "command not found" rather than adapting. The journal, /tmp and page-cache steps use journalctl, find and sysctl and work on any systemd distro. Full breakdown: Distro support.

Each is a separate prompt. The default answer is shown — Enter accepts it. # Step Command Default 1 apt cleanup apt autoremove --purge -y then apt clean Yes 2 Journal vacuum journalctl --vacuum-size=100M Yes 3 Snap revisions Removes disabled snap revisions Yes 4 Kernels Lists installed kernels — deletes nothing — 5 /tmp aging Removes files with atime older than 7 days Yes 6 Page cache sync then sysctl vm.drop_caches=3 No If sudo is unavailable the mode aborts immediately rather than running in a degraded state.

apt autoremove --purge -y removes packages nothing depends on any more, including superseded kernels. apt clean empties the downloaded .deb archive cache. This is the step that reclaims most of the space, typically 500 MB to 3 GB. The --purge means configuration files of removed packages go too.

Trims the systemd journal to 100 MB. This value is hardcoded and does not follow --days. The step first prints current journal usage so you can see whether it is worth doing. On a machine that has been up for a year the journal is often 1–4 GB.

Snap keeps old revisions of each package so you can roll back. This removes the ones already marked disabled, which are dead weight. The step is skipped cleanly when snap is not installed. Typically reclaims 1–5 GB on a snap-heavy Ubuntu install.

This step deletes nothing It prints the running kernel and lists installed linux-image-* packages for visibility. Removal of superseded kernels is handled by apt autoremove in step 1. Some third-party descriptions of this tool state that it removes old kernel packages directly. It does not — it shows you what is installed and leaves the removal to apt.

Removes files under /tmp whose atime is older than 7 days. Like the journal size, this threshold is hardcoded and does not follow --days. Most distros already clear /tmp on boot or via systemd-tmpfiles, so on a frequently-rebooted machine this reclaims very little.

sync followed by sysctl vm.drop_caches=3. This is the only step that defaults to No, and the only one that does not free disk space at all — it releases cached memory. It is harmless: the kernel repopulates the cache on demand. It is also close to pointless in normal operation, since the kernel already evicts cache under memory pressure. Its real use is making a memory measurement reproducible. Expect the machine to feel briefly slower afterwards as caches refill.

Does not hold a long-lived root session — each sudo call is separate and reviewable Does not edit /etc/sudoers Does not install, remove, enable or disable any service Does not touch /home or any user data Does not escalate silently — you will be prompted for your password by sudo itself

Step Typical reclaim apt 500 MB – 3 GB Journal 500 MB – 4 GB Snap 1 – 5 GB /tmp 0 – 500 MB Kernels 0 (listing only) Page cache 0 disk (frees RAM) Quarterly is a reasonable cadence. There is little point running it weekly — apt and journal growth is slow.
--system is step 8 of the guided walkthrough, so a full walkthrough already offers it. Skip it there with s if you would rather not enter a password mid-session, and run it separately later.
Distro support — what works outside Debian/Ubuntu Safety guards — how sudo is confined Reclaim the most space
--tui renders the category menu as a full-screen whiptail or dialog box. Added in 1.3.0. Same behaviour as --menu, different presentation. linux-cleanup --tui # or: -t, -g, --gui

Selecting an entry drops out of the dialog, runs that category with the normal CLI output and prompts, then returns to the menu. So the dialog is a launcher — the actual confirmations are still the standard text prompts, and every safety guard is unchanged. The TUI also carries an About dialog showing version, contact details, licence and the privacy guarantee.

Needs whiptail or dialog. If neither is present, the tool prints a per-distro install hint and falls back to the regular CLI menu — it does not fail. sudo apt install whiptail # Debian / Ubuntu sudo dnf install newt # Fedora / RHEL sudo pacman -S libnewt # Arch whiptail ships inside the newt / libnewt packages on RPM and Arch systems, which is why the package name does not match the command name. This is the only place the tool detects your distro The install hint above is distro-aware. Nothing else in linux-cleanup is — notably --system assumes Debian/Ubuntu.
--tui needs a terminal that can render a full-screen dialog. Over a constrained connection, inside a CI log, or in a ssh -T session without a TTY, use --menu instead — it needs nothing beyond bash.

Running linux-cleanup with no flags starts the guided walkthrough: ten steps through every cleanup category, each asking before it does anything. It is the recommended way to use the tool interactively. linux-cleanup # or: linux-cleanup -w / --walkthrough

# Step Deletes Notes 1 Package-manager caches Regenerable yarn, npm, npx, pnpm, pip, composer, bun, deno 2 Application caches Regenerable Browsers, Gradle, Cypress, Playwright, Zoom, editor VSIX 3 Developer-tool data Stale only Android AVDs, pub-cache, Dart analysis, flatpak 4 Editor old extensions Stale + superseded VS Code / Cursor 5 Stale node_modules Interactive Projects idle past the threshold 6 Partial / orphan downloads Interactive .crdownload, .part, .fdmdownload 7 Personal stale files Interactive Large idle files in ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop 8 System cleanup (sudo) System apt, journal, snap, /tmp, page cache 9 Final size audit Nothing Read-only summary 10 Generate readable report Nothing Markdown / HTML export — needs jq Steps 5, 6 and 7 are the interactive-only ones. They cannot be auto-confirmed, and step 7 is the only step in the whole tool that can remove something genuinely irreplaceable.

Two levels of confirmation. Per step, you choose what to do with the whole category: Key Effect a Run this step. This is the default — Enter selects it s Skip this step entirely q Quit the walkthrough now, keeping progress so far Per target, inside a step that you chose to run, each individual item gets a [Y/n] or [y/N] confirmation. The capitalised letter is the default. So a at the step level does not commit you to deleting everything in it — you still see and answer each target.

After each step that ran, the tool prints what that step freed and the session total so far: ✓ this step freed: 12.4 GB running total: 18.7 GB The final summary reports disk free before and after. That figure is measured from df, so it reflects everything happening on the machine — if a build ran during your session, the reported recovery can be lower than the sum of the steps, or even negative. That is not a bug; see Troubleshooting.

q at any step prompt, or Ctrl-C at any point, ends the session cleanly: The current removal finishes first — usually well under a second The log keeps everything up to that moment Ctrl-C exits with code 130, which the crash trap deliberately ignores, so no crash bundle is written Steps not reached are recorded as skipped in the report

Every walkthrough writes a canonical JSON report to ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-<timestamp>.json, containing per-step status and bytes freed, disk and memory before/after, and session totals. Full field list: Report schema. Step 10 optionally converts it to Markdown and HTML. That step needs jq; without it the step is recorded as skipped (jq missing) and the JSON is still written. linux-cleanup --no-report # skip JSON generation; logs still written

linux-cleanup -d 30 # 30-day staleness threshold instead of 100 linux-cleanup --purge-all # disable the staleness gate entirely linux-cleanup --no-color # plain output linux-cleanup --cleanup-logs # delete this run's log at the end --purge-all changes what step 1–4 delete With the staleness gate off, cache steps wipe their targets in full rather than pruning idle files. That includes Gradle wrapper distributions, Playwright browsers and Cypress binaries you may still want. The pre-run banner states which strategy is active.

linux-cleanup has no undo. This page is about working out what was removed and what your real options are. Stop writing to the disk first If something irreplaceable was deleted and you intend to attempt file-carving recovery, stop using the filesystem now. Every write reduces the chance of recovering unlinked data. That applies only to the genuinely irreplaceable categories. For a cache, skip it — just let the tool re-fetch.

Two artefacts, written on every run. Both are records, not backups. # The most recent session log — every path touched, with sizes less "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-*.log | head -1)" # The structured record of the same session jq '.' "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" To search for a specific path across every session you have ever run: grep -rn 'the-filename-you-are-missing' ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/ If nothing matches, linux-cleanup did not delete it. The log records every removal attempt, including the refusals. That is worth checking before assuming this tool is the cause. Narrow to a single session's steps: jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran")' \ "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)"
