documents.t: Refusals are logged too. If you find a line like this, nothing was deleted: ✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/notes See Protected paths.
documents.s: 2. Confirm it was not simply refused

documents.t: What was deleted Recovery Package-manager cache Automatic. The next install re-downloads it Browser cache Automatic. Rebuilds as you browse Gradle cache or wrapper distro Automatic. Next build re-fetches — expect a slow first build Cypress / Playwright binaries Re-run the install step for that tool node_modules yarn install or npm install in the project Android AVD Recreate in Android Studio. The profile config is gone; the system image re-downloads Editor extension version Reload the editor window; reinstall if genuinely missing apt cache, journal, snap revisions Regenerate on their own. Nothing to do Personal file from ~/Downloads Only from your own backup, or re-download from the source Partial download Not recoverable. Restart the download

# In the affected project yarn install # or: npm install / pnpm install # Test-runner binaries npx cypress install npx playwright install # Flutter flutter pub get Nothing here needs the tool's involvement — you are just letting each tool do what it does on a cold cache.

Realistically, in order: Your own backup. Timeshift, Borg, restic, rsync snapshot, cloud sync — whatever you run. This is the only reliable answer. The original source. A downloaded file can be downloaded again. Check your browser history for the URL. A sync service's trash. Dropbox, Nextcloud, Google Drive and similar keep deleted files server-side for a retention window. If the directory was synced, look there. File-carving tools — extundelete, testdisk, photorec. These work on unlinked inodes and are a long shot on a busy filesystem, especially SSDs with TRIM enabled. Unmount the filesystem first, or work from a live USB, and never write recovered data back to the same device. Be honest with yourself about step 4 On a mounted, actively-used SSD with TRIM, carving usually recovers nothing. It is worth attempting only for something genuinely important, and only after you have stopped writing to the disk.

Change Effect Run --scan before every cleanup You see the outcome while it is still hypothetical Move valuables out of ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop ~/Documents and friends are protected Skip step 7 in the walkthrough Personal files then need a deliberate separate run Raise the threshold: -d 365 Only genuinely ancient files become candidates Never use -y outside --all-safe on a trusted machine -y cannot touch personal data, but you see decisions only afterwards Set up a real backup The only thing that makes any deletion recoverable

If a deletion happened inside a protected path, or a current editor extension version was removed, or anything else contradicts the documented guards — that is a bug worth reporting. linux-cleanup --debug-bundle linux-cleanup --feedback Include the log and the session record. See Send a bug report.

Every environment variable linux-cleanup reads. All are optional. Variable Default Effect NO_COLOR unset Any non-empty value disables ANSI colour. The cross-tool standard from no-color.org. Same as --no-color CLEANUP_NO_COLOR 0 linux-cleanup-specific colour switch. Set to 1 to disable colour here only LINUX_CLEANUP_LOG_DIR ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/ (npx / npm) or <repo>/logs/ (clone) Where session logs go. Created if missing LINUX_CLEANUP_REPORTS_DIR ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/ or <repo>/reports/ Where JSON session records go. Created if missing LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME unset — falls back to the parent of the log dir Parent for logs/, reports/ and feedback/ together LINUX_CLEANUP_NPX unset Internal. Set to 1 by the Node launcher. Do not set it yourself XDG_CONFIG_HOME ~/.config Where personal-roots.txt and project-roots.txt are looked up

LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME is the single lever that moves everything — logs, records and feedback bundles: export LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME="/mnt/secure/linux-cleanup" linux-cleanup --scan The directory is created, the mount is not The tool creates logs/, reports/ and feedback/ beneath the path you give it. It does not create or verify the underlying mount point. Point this at an unmounted path and output lands on the underlying filesystem instead — quietly. Verify the target is mounted and writable before relying on it. For finer control, LINUX_CLEANUP_LOG_DIR and LINUX_CLEANUP_REPORTS_DIR override individually and take precedence over the data home.

export NO_COLOR=1 # everything on this machine, all tools export CLEANUP_NO_COLOR=1 # only linux-cleanup linux-cleanup --no-color # only this invocation CLEANUP_NO_COLOR exists for the case where you want colour from every other tool and plain output from this one — typically when piping its output somewhere that mangles escape sequences.

Two files under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default ~/.config) control which directories the personal and project scanners walk: File Used by Default roots personal-roots.txt --stale ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop project-roots.txt --node-modules Your project directories One path per line. This follows the XDG Base Directory specification, so setting XDG_CONFIG_HOME relocates both. Adding a root to personal-roots.txt widens what can be deleted The personal scanner is interactive-only, so nothing is removed without your per-file confirmation — but a root you add is a directory whose contents will start appearing in candidate lists. The path allowlist still applies and still wins: adding ~/Documents here does not make it deletable.
NO_COLOR=1 linux-cleanup --scan --no-report > /tmp/scan.log --no-report skips JSON generation when only the log matters. Check the exit code rather than parsing output.

PATH, except to detect which optional tools are installed USER and LOGNAME, except to annotate the log header Your shell history, aliases or configuration — --doctor is the only mode that reads shell-init files, and only to check whether a runtime is wired in Any remote or network-provided configuration. There is none If $HOME is unset the script aborts immediately rather than guessing. See Troubleshooting.
Output paths — where files actually land CLI flags
linux-cleanup follows the Unix convention: 0 is success, anything else is a problem. Some non-zero codes are expected and deliberately not treated as crashes.

Code Meaning Crash bundle 0 Clean run. Every requested action completed or was declined No 1 Generic failure — an invariant was violated. Rare Yes 2 Argument parse error. Help is printed No 127 Command not found — a required dependency is missing Yes 130 Aborted with Ctrl-C (SIGINT) No 137 Killed by SIGKILL — usually the OOM killer or kill -9 Yes 139 Segfault. Should not happen in pure bash Yes 143 Terminated by SIGTERM No any other non-zero Unexpected internal failure Yes 2 is the one worth remembering: an unknown flag exits 2. If you typed --dry-run expecting safety, this is the code you get — and no cleanup runs. That is not a safety feature to rely on; use --scan.

The EXIT trap added in 1.3.0 evaluates in this order: Exit code is 0, or the script set its internal completion sentinel → no bundle Exit code is 130 (Ctrl-C) or 143 (SIGTERM) → no bundle. A user-initiated stop is not a crash Exit code is 2 (argument parse) → no bundle. The script printed help and stopped on purpose Anything else → write crash-<timestamp>.tar.gz to ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/ The bundle contains the active session log, the most recent JSON record, and a short system manifest. It stays on your machine — nothing is transmitted. The tool prints the path so you can review it and decide whether to email it. See Send a bug report.

if linux-cleanup --scan; then echo "scan succeeded" else case $? in 2) echo "bad flag" ;; 127) echo "missing dependency — run --self-test" ;; 130) echo "user aborted" ;; *) echo "unexpected failure — check ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/" ;; esac fi

linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --no-report --cleanup-logs >>~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log 2>&1 || \ echo "linux-cleanup exited $?" | mail -s "cleanup failed on $(hostname)" you@example.com Exit code 127 from a cron job almost always means the crontab used a bare command name and cron's minimal PATH could not find it. Use an absolute path — see Troubleshooting.

The bundle's manifest records the exit code. The common ones: Code Usual cause 137 Out-of-memory killer. Typically a find over an enormous tree 141 SIGPIPE — a pipe closed early, often a tee or pager exiting 139 Segfault — should never occur here; report it 127 Missing dependency. Run --self-test to identify it

All output lives under one data root. Which root depends on how you installed the tool, and both can be overridden.

$DATA_HOME/ ├── logs/ │ ├── cleanup-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.log # one per session │ └── cron.log # appended by the weekly cron ├── reports/ │ ├── report-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.json # canonical session record │ ├── report-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.md # created by --export md │ └── report-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.html # created by --export html └── feedback/ ├── debug-bundle-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.tar.gz # created by --debug-bundle └── crash-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.tar.gz # created automatically on a crash

Installed via $DATA_HOME npx linux-cleanup ~/.linux-cleanup/ npm install -g linux-cleanup ~/.linux-cleanup/ git clone The clone directory itself The difference is deliberate. npx runs the package from a temporary npm cache directory that gets evicted, so writing output there would lose it; ~/.linux-cleanup/ persists across runs. A clone is already a permanent location, so output stays beside the source. Override either with LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME, or the log and record directories individually.

Path Auto-cleaned Notes logs/cleanup-*.log Only with --cleanup-logs That flag deletes this run's log at finish. Past logs stay logs/cron.log Never Never rotated. Rotate it yourself if it grows reports/*.json Never The durable audit trail reports/*.md, *.html Never Created on demand, removed on demand feedback/*.tar.gz Never You decide when they are no longer needed --cleanup-logs is the only automatic deletion the tool performs on its own output, and it only ever touches .log files.

Artefact Typical Session log 50–500 KB JSON record 5–50 KB Feedback or crash bundle 50–200 KB A year of weekly cron runs totals a few megabytes. To thin older files: find ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/ -name 'cleanup-*.log' -mtime +90 -delete find ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/ -name 'report-*' -mtime +90 -delete Rotating the cron log: mv ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log.old touch ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log
Artefact Mode Logs and records 0644 Feedback bundles 0640 logs/, reports/ 0755 feedback/ 0750 All owned by the invoking user. The tool does not chown or chmod anything outside $DATA_HOME.

Logs and bundles contain your paths A session log names every path touched, which means it contains directory names from your machine — project names, and sometimes filenames from ~/Downloads. That is local-only and never transmitted, but review a bundle before emailing it: tar -tzf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-*.tar.gz See Send a bug report. Nothing here contains file contents — only paths, sizes and timestamps. These are records of what happened, not copies of what was deleted. See Recovery.

These are the paths linux-cleanup refuses to delete. The refusal is unconditional — there is no flag that overrides it, including --purge-all. Every candidate is resolved with realpath before the check, so a symlink pointing into a protected directory is refused on the resolved path, not the link. Verify against your own install rather than trusting this page Lists change between versions, and second-hand descriptions of this tool circulate with directories that are not actually protected. linux-cleanup --list-targets # the lists as your build sees them linux-cleanup --self-test # asserts the guard fires on known paths

The guard is built from three lists with different matching rules. The distinction matters — it is what lets ~/.npm/_cacache be cleaned while ~/.npm itself is untouchable. List Matches Purpose Protected paths The path and everything beneath it Personal data, credentials, configuration Protected exact Only that exact path Package-manager install roots Protected basenames Any file with that name, anywhere Shell-init and history files

Refused as a path or as any child, except where noted. Path Children also refused / — (root itself) /home No — only the exact path /root No — only the exact path /etc Yes /boot Yes /usr Yes /var No — only the exact path /lib No — only the exact path /sbin No — only the exact path /bin No — only the exact path $HOME No — the home root itself, so a bare $HOME can never be wiped /proc and /sys are not on this list No cleanup target goes anywhere near them, but the allowlist does not name them explicitly. Some descriptions of this tool claim it does. It does not.

Refused along with everything inside them. Path Holds ~/Documents Documents ~/Pictures Images ~/Music Audio ~/Videos Video ~/Desktop Desktop contents ~/Public Shared files ~/Templates Document templates ~/Downloads is deliberately NOT protected It cannot be — cleaning large, long-idle files there is a feature (Stale personal files). What protects it instead is Guard 3: interactive-only, per-file confirmation, and --yes ignored. If you keep anything irreplaceable in ~/Downloads, move it into a protected directory. That is the durable fix.

Path Holds ~/.ssh SSH keys and known hosts ~/.gnupg GPG keyring ~/.config Application configuration (very broad) ~/.gnome GNOME settings ~/.mozilla Firefox profiles ~/.thunderbird Thunderbird profiles ~/.claude Claude Code state ~/.local/share/claude Claude Code data Two paths commonly claimed as protected are NOT ~/.password-store (pass) and ~/.aws (AWS credentials) do not appear on the protected list in the source. Some write-ups of this tool state that they do. In practice no cleanup target points at either, so neither is at risk during normal operation — but do not rely on the allowlist to defend them. If you want that guarantee, verify with --list-targets on your own install first. Note that ~/.mozilla being protected does not stop Firefox cache cleanup: the cache lives under ~/.cache/mozilla, a different tree.

Matched exactly — children remain cleanable. This is what preserves your globally installed packages while still allowing the regenerable cache inside each install root to be pruned. Ecosystem Paths pnpm ~/.local/share/pnpm and its global, bin, nodejs npm ~/.npm, ~/.npm-global, ~/.npm-global/lib, ~/.npm-global/lib/node_modules yarn ~/.yarn, ~/.config/yarn/global bun ~/.bun, ~/.bun/install, ~/.bun/install/global and its node_modules, ~/.bun/bin deno ~/.deno, ~/.deno/bin Node version managers ~/.volta, ~/.volta/bin, ~/.nvm, ~/.nvm/versions, ~/.fnm Rust ~/.cargo, ~/.cargo/bin, ~/.rustup Go ~/go, ~/go/bin This list exists because of a real defect: before 1.1.0 the pnpm cleanup targeted ~/.local/share/pnpm — the install root — and removed globally installed packages along with the pnpm binary itself. The fix narrowed the target to ~/.local/share/pnpm/store and added this list so the mistake cannot recur. --all-safe additionally asserts at startup that none of these ever appear in its target list, aborting with a BUG: message if one does.

Refused by filename, in any location, regardless of the path leading to it: .bashrc · .bash_profile · .bash_login · .profile · .bash_logout · .zshrc · .zshenv · .zprofile · .zlogin · .zlogout · .bash_aliases · .bash_history · .zsh_history · .inputrc · .dircolors · .config · .local This is a last-ditch guard. It exists so a future bug that somehow introduced a shell-init file into a target list still cannot delete it.

✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/notes ✗ REFUSE: unsafe path: '/home/you' ✗ REFUSE: shell-init / history file: /home/you/.bashrc A refusal is correct behaviour, not an error to work around. If a cache you want cleaned is being refused, the cause is almost always a symlink landing somewhere protected — fix the symlink, not the tool. See Troubleshooting.
Safety guards — how this list is applied What it deletes — the other side of the boundary

Every session writes a JSON record with "schema_version": 1. This page documents the structure the tool actually emits, verified against the source of 1.4.0. Older documentation describes a different structure Some material — including a reference page inside the source repository — describes a shape built around schema (a string like linux-cleanup/report/v1) with tool, session and categories objects. The tool does not emit that. A parser written against it will fail on every real file. The structure below is what modules/walkthrough.sh writes. Confirm on your own machine: jq 'keys' "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)"

{ "schema_version": 1, "credits": { }, "meta": { }, "disk": { "before": {}, "after": {} }, "memory": { "before": {}, "after": {} }, "steps": [ ], "totals": { } } Key Type Holds schema_version number Currently 1. Reject anything you do not recognise credits object Tool identity, licence and author meta object Session context — when, where, how, with what settings disk object Filesystem usage before and after memory object Memory usage before and after steps array One entry per step attempted totals object Session summary

{ "tool": "linux-cleanup", "tool_version": "1.4.0", "tool_homepage": "https://aoneahsan.com", "tool_license": "MIT", "author": { "name": "Ahsan Mahmood", "email": "aoneahsan@gmail.com", "website": "https://aoneahsan.com", "linkedin": "https://linkedin.com/in/aoneahsan" } } Present so a record is self-attributing wherever it ends up. Nothing here reflects your machine.

Key Type Holds tool string Always linux-cleanup tool_version string The version that wrote the record. Gate consumer logic on this started_at string Session start timestamp finished_at string Session end timestamp duration_seconds number Wall-clock duration host string hostname output user string $USER mode string The mode that ran — walkthrough, scan, allsafe, system, and so on stale_days number The --days threshold in force log_file string Absolute path to this session's log launcher string How it was invoked — bash for a direct run via_npx number 1 when run through the npm launcher, 0 otherwise stale_days is worth capturing: it is the difference between a run that pruned at 100 days and one that ran with -d 30, and it explains why two sessions on the same machine reclaimed different amounts.

Both hold a before and an after snapshot, taken at session start and end. disk carries filesystem fields — filesystem, size, used, available and use percentage — derived from df. memory carries the equivalent from the system's memory report. after minus before is not purely your cleanup These are whole-machine measurements. A build, a package update or a browser running during the session moves them too, which is why a reported recovery can be lower than the sum of the steps — or negative. See Troubleshooting.

An array, one entry per step attempted, in order: { "n": 1, "title": "Package-manager caches", "status": "ran", "freed_bytes": 13315108864 } Key Type Holds n number 1-based step number title string Human-readable step name status string ran, skipped, skipped (quit), or skipped (jq missing) freed_bytes number Bytes reclaimed by this step. 0 when skipped skipped (quit) marks the steps after you pressed q — useful for telling a deliberate stop from a step you declined individually.
Key Type Holds total_reclaimed_bytes number Sum across steps total_reclaimed_human string The same, formatted steps_run number Steps with status ran steps_skipped number Steps with a skipped status

LATEST="$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" jq '.totals.total_reclaimed_human' "$LATEST" jq '.meta | {mode, stale_days, duration_seconds}' "$LATEST" jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran") | "\(.title): \(.freed_bytes)"' "$LATEST" # Reclaim across every session on record jq -s 'map(.totals.total_reclaimed_bytes) | add' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json

No JSON Schema file ships with the tool. A structural check: jq -e 'has("schema_version") and .schema_version == 1 and has("meta") and has("steps") and has("totals")' \ ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json Prints true per valid file.

Writing a consumer: Branch on schema_version. Treat an unfamiliar value as unparseable rather than guessing Treat unknown keys as additive. Fields have been added within version 1 and may be again Use meta.tool_version for behaviour that differs between releases Do not assume every mode fills every section. Read-only modes produce fewer steps Expect total_reclaimed_bytes to be negative occasionally. It is a df delta, not a sum of deletions
Reports — viewing and exporting Output paths — where the files live

linux-cleanup applies up to four independent gates before any deletion. A path must clear every gate that applies to it. This page explains what each gate is, why it exists, and what it does not cover. The guards are the entire safety model. There is no backup and no undo behind them.

Always on. Cannot be disabled, and no flag overrides it. Before any removal, the target is resolved with realpath and rejected if it lands on or inside a protected path. Because resolution happens first, a symlink cannot smuggle a path through: if ~/.cache/yarn is a symlink into ~/Documents, the resolved path is inside ~/Documents, the guard fires, and the deletion is refused. Three separate lists back this up: List Match style Purpose System roots and personal directories Path or any child /etc, ~/Documents, ~/.ssh, ~/.config, … Package-manager install roots Exact path only ~/.local/share/pnpm, ~/.npm, ~/.cargo, … Shell-init and history files Basename, any location .bashrc, .zshrc, .bash_history, … When the guard fires you see a refusal on stderr: ✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/notes The exact-match list deserves a note. ~/.npm is protected exactly, which is what allows ~/.npm/_cacache — a child — to be cleaned. That is deliberate: the install root is preserved while the regenerable cache inside it is fair game. The full lists are at Protected paths. What this guard does not do It protects locations, not value. A 40 GB irreplaceable video sitting in ~/Downloads is not covered by the allowlist — ~/Downloads is not a protected path. It is covered by Guard 3 instead. Why an allowlist rather than a blocklist. A blocklist fails open: anything the author forgot to list is deletable, so one typo in a path is the difference between clearing a cache and clearing a home directory. An allowlist fails closed — an unrecognised path is refused by default. For a tool that runs rm -rf at scale with sudo available, failing closed is the only defensible default.

Default: 100 days. Introduced in 1.2.0, extended in 1.2.1. Since 1.2.0 the default strategy is to prune, not wipe. Within a target directory, a file is deleted only when both its atime and its mtime are older than --days. Empty directories left behind are swept up; the directory shell itself stays so the owning tool still finds its layout. Requiring both timestamps matters. mtime alone would delete a file downloaded a year ago and read yesterday; atime alone is unreliable on filesystems mounted noatime or relatime. Requiring both is the conservative reading. For anything that is a tool rather than a cache — Android AVDs, editor extension versions, flatpak user data — 1.2.1 added a second condition on top. Such an asset is removed only when no active software depends on it AND it has been idle past the threshold. Each asset is evaluated as an indivisible unit, so a partial prune cannot leave a half-deleted emulator profile behind. linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -d 30 # more aggressive: 30-day threshold linux-cleanup --all-safe -y # default: 100 days linux-cleanup --all-safe --purge-all # gate OFF — full wipe, pre-1.2.0 behaviour --purge-all disables this guard entirely With --purge-all every target cache is wiped in full regardless of age. That is the behaviour that prompted the gate: it removes Gradle wrapper distributions, Playwright browsers for old release branches, and yarn-cached tarballs of pinned dependencies — each an expensive re-download. It is a legitimate choice before reimaging a machine. It is a poor default for everyday use. The pre-run banner states which strategy is active, so there is never any ambiguity about what is about to happen.

The modes that can touch personal files are interactive by policy: --stale — large, idle files in ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop --partials — orphaned partial downloads --node-modules — stale project dependency directories --yes does not apply to these modes and never will. --yes auto-confirms regenerable caches only. The tool prints its candidate list, waits for per-entry confirmation, and deletes nothing until you answer. The reasoning is that personal files carry no signal a program can read. Nothing on disk distinguishes an installer you will never open again from the only copy of a document you have not needed yet. The user is the only oracle, so the tool refuses to guess.
documents.s: Guard 3 — Personal data is interactive only

documents.t: --system is the only mode that calls sudo, and it does so for a fixed, enumerated set of operations — each a separate, reviewable invocation, each prompted individually: Operation Prompt default apt autoremove --purge -y and apt clean Yes journalctl --vacuum-size=100M Yes Remove disabled snap revisions Yes List installed kernels — no deletion — Remove /tmp files with atime older than 7 days Yes sync then sysctl vm.drop_caches=3 No The script does not hold a long-lived root session, does not edit /etc/sudoers, does not install or modify any service, and never escalates silently. If sudo is unavailable the mode aborts rather than continuing in a degraded state. Two values here are hardcoded and ignore --days: the journal vacuum target (100 MB) and the /tmp age threshold (7 days).

Being explicit about the gaps is more useful than reassurance. Gap What it means No undo Nothing here makes a deletion reversible. See Deletion is permanent. ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop are not allowlisted They are reachable. Only Guard 3 stands between them and deletion — read the candidates. --purge-all removes Guard 2 Guards 1, 3 and 4 still apply; the staleness gate does not. Running as root widens the blast radius The tool is designed to run as a normal user. --system handles the legitimate sudo needs internally. Guards protect paths, not content A protected directory is safe wherever it sits; a valuable file outside one is not. /proc and /sys are not on the protected list Nothing targets them, but the allowlist does not name them either.

npx linux-cleanup --self-test # asserts the guards fire on known paths npx linux-cleanup --list-targets # prints both target and protected lists --self-test is the honest check. It asserts that /, $HOME, ~/Documents, ~/.ssh and /etc are protected and that ~/.cache/yarn is not, then exits non-zero if any assertion fails. Documentation can drift; the assertion runs against the code you actually have.
Protected paths — the complete verified lists Deletion is permanent — the model behind "no undo" What it deletes — the target inventory

linux-cleanup calls rm -rf. There is no undo, no trash directory, no snapshot, and no backup step. Once a path is removed, this tool cannot bring it back, and neither can any flag you pass it. Read this before your first destructive run Deleted files do not go to a trash or recycle bin. There is no --undo, no restore command, and no hidden copy kept anywhere. The session log and JSON report record what was deleted, not the data itself. If a file was irreplaceable and you had no backup, it is gone. The tool's safety comes entirely from refusing to delete the wrong thing in the first place.

Most of what this tool removes is described as regenerable. That word is doing precise work, and it is worth being exact about what it does and does not mean. It means It does not mean Some other program can recreate the data linux-cleanup can recreate it The next yarn install re-downloads the package The bytes are still on your disk somewhere The browser rebuilds its cache as you browse The deletion is reversible Recreation may need network, time, or both Recreation is free or instant A Playwright browser bundle is regenerable — and re-downloading it takes several minutes and a few hundred megabytes of bandwidth. An offline machine cannot regenerate it at all. Regenerable is a statement about where the data can come from, not about how convenient it is to get back.

Three targets are not regenerable in any sense. All three are interactive-only, and all three deserve real attention when you are answering prompts. Target Why nothing can bring it back Personal files in ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop No source to re-fetch from. If it was the only copy, that was the copy. Partial downloads (.crdownload, .part, …) Resumable only by the original browser session, which is usually long gone. Uncommitted work inside a stale node_modules Rare, but a patched dependency you edited in place is not in any registry. The first is the one that costs people data. ~/Downloads is not a protected path — it cannot be, since cleaning it is a core feature — so the only thing standing between a file there and deletion is you reading the candidate list.
documents.s: The categories that are genuinely irreplaceable

documents.t: The design rationale, stated plainly: An undo log is write amplification on the disk you are trying to free. Preserving 20 GB in order to reclaim 20 GB accomplishes nothing. It would create false confidence. A tool that appears reversible invites careless use, and the reversibility would be partial at best — an undo that restores 90% of cases is most dangerous in the other 10%. Prevention is a better investment than recovery. The allowlist, staleness gate and interactive confirmation stop the bad deletion from happening, which is strictly better than undoing it afterwards. This is a reasonable trade for caches. It is a trade you should understand before pointing the tool at ~/Downloads.

If a deletion surprises you, two artefacts exist. Both are records, not backups. Artefact Location Contains Session log ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-<timestamp>.log Every path touched, its size, and the result of each removal JSON report ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-<timestamp>.json The same information, structured and schema-versioned They tell you exactly what was removed and when — which is what you need to decide whether to restore from your own backup, re-download, or file a bug. They contain none of the deleted content. Full procedure: Recovery.

# 1. Confirm the guards work on this install npx linux-cleanup --self-test # 2. See what would be reclaimed — deletes nothing npx linux-cleanup --scan # 3. Run guided, answering 'n' to anything you are unsure about npx linux-cleanup Beyond that: Have a backup of anything irreplaceable. This is true regardless of this tool; it is simply the only thing that makes any deletion recoverable. Never point the personal-file modes at a machine you have not audited. Run --scan first. Keep --all-safe -y for caches on machines you already trust. It cannot touch personal files, but it also shows you nothing until it finishes. Treat --purge-all as a pre-reimage tool, not a daily driver. The one habit worth forming Run --scan before --all-safe, every time. It costs a minute and it is the only step that shows you the outcome while it is still hypothetical.
documents.s: Reducing the risk before you run

documents.t: Recovery — the procedure after an unwanted deletion Safety guards — what prevents the deletion in the first place Preview before deleting — the read-only modes

linux-cleanup has no --dry-run flag. Previewing is done with three separate read-only modes. None of them deletes anything, and running all three takes about a minute. Why there is no --dry-run A --dry-run flag usually pairs with a destructive command that runs the same code path either way. Here the read-only work is a genuinely different mode — --scan walks and measures, --list-targets enumerates configuration, neither shares a code path with deletion. The practical consequence: adding --dry-run to a cleanup command does nothing and will not protect you. Unknown flags exit with code 2, so the command simply fails — but do not rely on that as a safety net. Use --scan.

Run them in this order. Each answers a different question. npx linux-cleanup --self-test # Are the safety guards actually working? npx linux-cleanup --list-targets # What paths could this ever touch? npx linux-cleanup --scan # What would it reclaim on THIS machine, right now?

Verifies required dependencies, checks the syntax of every shell file, and asserts that the protection logic returns the right answer for known paths: /, $HOME, ~/Documents, ~/.ssh and /etc must be protected, while ~/.cache/yarn must not be. A single failed assertion aborts with a non-zero exit code. A clean run ends with a pass message. This is the cheapest possible way to confirm the copy you downloaded behaves as documented. Run it after every install or upgrade.

Prints every path the script is capable of targeting, grouped by category, plus the protected paths it refuses. This is configuration, not a measurement — it does not stat your disk and does not care what actually exists. Use it to answer "is my X in scope?" without running anything.

The one that matters most. --scan walks every category, measures real sizes on your machine, and prints what each would reclaim. It writes a JSON report and deletes nothing. npx linux-cleanup --scan Typical output on a developer laptop: Category Typical range Yarn + npm + pnpm caches 5–25 GB Browser profile caches 2–8 GB ~/.gradle/caches 3–10 GB Cypress + Playwright binaries 1–4 GB Android emulator images 6–30 GB Stale node_modules 5–50 GB A scan is a snapshot, not a promise The numbers are what exists at scan time. By the time you run the real cleanup, the staleness gate may exclude files that a running build has just touched — so the amount actually reclaimed is often lower than the scan suggested. That is the gate doing its job.

Three things are worth checking in the output: Anything under a path you did not expect. If a cache lives behind a symlink into a directory you care about, this is where you see it. Investigate with realpath before proceeding. Anything in the Expensive column. Gradle wrapper distributions, Cypress and Playwright binaries, and Android AVDs cost real time to re-download. See What it deletes. The personal-file candidates. These are the only entries that can be irreplaceable. Read every one.
documents.s: Reading a scan before acting on it

documents.t: Several modes are read-only in their own right and can be run individually: Command Shows Deletes --scan Every cache category with sizes Never --audit The 20 largest entries in $HOME Never --globals Global npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/deno packages Never --list-targets Every targetable path Never --self-test Dependency and guard checks Never The interactive modes — --node-modules, --stale, --partials — print their full candidate list before asking for confirmation, so they double as a preview if you answer no to everything. Nothing is removed until you say yes.

When the scan looks right, the safest first run is the guided walkthrough with no flags: npx linux-cleanup It asks before every step and before every target. Answer n to anything that surprises you, s to skip a whole step, or q to quit — partial progress is kept in the log and report. Do not start with --all-safe -y --all-safe -y skips every confirmation for regenerable caches. It is the right tool for a weekly cron job on a machine you already trust. It is the wrong way to meet this tool for the first time, because you will not see what it decided until it is finished.

linux-cleanup removes regenerable data: files a tool will rebuild or re-download the next time it needs them. This page is the complete inventory, grouped by how expensive each category is to get back. Every deletion on this page is permanent. "Regenerable" means a program can recreate it, not that linux-cleanup can. Get this list from your own machine The authoritative list for your system, with real paths and real sizes, comes from the tool itself: npx linux-cleanup --list-targets # every path it can touch npx linux-cleanup --scan # those paths, with current sizes, deleting nothing

Regeneration cost Meaning Free Rebuilt automatically, in seconds, without you noticing Cheap Re-downloaded on next use; costs bandwidth and a short wait Expensive Large re-download or long rebuild — minutes to hours Manual Nothing regenerates it. Gone means gone
documents.s: How to read the cost column

documents.t: Downloaded archives kept so a reinstall skips the network. Deleting them slows the next install and nothing else. Target Path Typical size Cost Yarn v1 ~/.cache/yarn 2–20 GB Cheap Yarn Berry ~/.yarn/berry/cache 1–8 GB Cheap npm ~/.npm/_cacache 1–10 GB Cheap npx ~/.npm/_npx 100 MB–2 GB Cheap pnpm store ~/.local/share/pnpm/store 2–15 GB Cheap pip ~/.cache/pip 200 MB–3 GB Cheap Composer ~/.composer/cache 100 MB–2 GB Cheap bun ~/.bun/install/cache 100 MB–2 GB Cheap deno ~/.cache/deno 100 MB–2 GB Cheap The install directories are protected, only the caches are cleaned ~/.local/share/pnpm (which holds your globally installed packages and the pnpm binary itself), ~/.npm, ~/.yarn, ~/.bun/install/global and ~/.deno/bin are on the exact-match protected list. Only the regenerable store or cache inside them is targeted. This distinction was a real bug: before 1.1.0 the pnpm cleanup targeted ~/.local/share/pnpm and wiped globally installed packages. See the changelog.

Target Path Typical size Cost Chrome / Chromium / Brave / Edge / Vivaldi profile Cache/ dirs 500 MB–8 GB Free Firefox / Mozilla cache2/ 500 MB–4 GB Free Gradle build cache ~/.gradle/caches 3–10 GB Cheap Gradle wrapper distributions ~/.gradle/wrapper/dists 200 MB–3 GB Expensive Cypress binaries ~/.cache/Cypress 500 MB–3 GB Expensive Playwright browsers ~/.cache/ms-playwright 500 MB–3 GB Expensive TypeScript watcher cache project-local small Free Zoom data ~/.zoom/Cache 100 MB–2 GB Free VS Code / Cursor cached VSIX ~/.config/Code/CachedExtensionVSIXs 100 MB–1 GB Cheap Browser caches are the safest thing on this page — your history, bookmarks, passwords and sessions live in different files that are never targeted. Expect slightly slower first page loads afterwards. The three Expensive rows are exactly why the staleness gate exists. A Gradle wrapper distribution is a 230 MB download you might need again next month, so by default it survives unless it has been idle for 100+ days.

Not caches — actual installed tooling. These clear the highest bar: a dependency check and the staleness gate. Target Path Typical size Cost Android emulator images (AVDs) ~/.android/avd 6–30 GB Expensive Flutter pub cache ~/.pub-cache 1–5 GB Cheap Dart analysis server cache ~/.dartServer 100 MB–1 GB Free Flatpak user data ~/.local/share/flatpak 1–10 GB Expensive Each AVD is treated as an indivisible unit: its .avd directory and sibling .ini are examined together and pruned only when every file in the profile is idle past the threshold. An emulator you booted last month survives. Flatpak is stricter still — the module refuses to touch the tree at all if any user-scope app is installed, and points you at flatpak uninstall --user --unused instead.

Superseded VS Code and Cursor extension versions: the older copies left behind when an extension updates. Removal requires both that a newer version exists and that the old version has been idle past the threshold. The current version of an extension is never a candidate. See Editor extensions.

These are never batched and never auto-confirmed. --yes has no effect on them, by design. Target What it finds Cost Stale node_modules Project directories untouched for N+ days Cheap (yarn install) Partial downloads *.fdmdownload, *.crdownload, *.part Manual Stale personal files Files in ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop over 10 MB and idle N+ days Manual The personal-file modes are the only ones that can delete something irreplaceable node_modules and partial downloads are throwaway by nature. Files in ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop are not — the tool has no way to tell an installer you will never open again from the only copy of a document. That is precisely why these modes require you to confirm each entry by hand, and why --yes is ignored here. Read each candidate. See Stale personal files.
documents.s: Project and personal files — interactive only

documents.t: Only runs under --system, and each step asks first. Step What it does Default answer apt apt autoremove --purge -y then apt clean Yes Journal journalctl --vacuum-size=100M — hardcoded, not --days Yes Snap Removes disabled snap revisions Yes Kernels Lists installed kernels only. Deletes nothing — /tmp Removes files with atime older than 7 days — hardcoded, not --days Yes Page cache sync then vm.drop_caches=3 — frees RAM, not disk No --system is Debian/Ubuntu only The apt steps call apt and dpkg directly with no distro detection and no command -v guard. On Fedora, Arch or openSUSE they fail with "command not found" rather than adapting. Everything else on this page works on any distro. Details: Distro support.

The allowlist is a hard refusal with no override flag. Any path resolving inside these is rejected, after realpath resolution so a symlink cannot smuggle a path past the check. Category Paths System roots /, /home, /root, /etc, /boot, /usr, /var, /lib, /sbin, /bin Home root $HOME itself Personal data ~/Documents, ~/Pictures, ~/Music, ~/Videos, ~/Desktop, ~/Public, ~/Templates Credentials ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg Configuration ~/.config, ~/.gnome, ~/.mozilla, ~/.thunderbird Agent state ~/.claude, ~/.local/share/claude Shell init Any file named .bashrc, .zshrc, .profile, .bash_aliases, .bash_history, and similar Verify this list against your own install Protected-path lists drift between versions, and some third-party write-ups of this tool list directories that are not actually protected — ~/.password-store and ~/.aws among them. Do not trust any document, including this one, over your own machine: npx linux-cleanup --list-targets npx linux-cleanup --self-test # asserts the guards actually fire The complete verified list is at Protected paths.
Preview before deleting — see the outcome before committing to it Safety guards — the four gates, and what each one is for Deletion is permanent — what to do when something surprises you
Symptom → cause → fix. Run the verify command first; if it matches, apply the fix. If you have lost data rather than hit an error, go to Recovery instead.

✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/something Cause. The path resolved — after symlink expansion — to somewhere on the protected list. The allowlist blocked it. This is correct behaviour, not a failure. Nothing was deleted. Fix. Find out what resolved where: linux-cleanup --list-targets realpath <the path that was rejected> Almost always a cache symlinked into a protected directory. Fix the symlink, not the tool — the tool is doing exactly its job. There is no override flag, by design. Two related messages: ✗ REFUSE: unsafe path: '/home/you' # bare $HOME or / ✗ REFUSE: shell-init / history file: … # .bashrc, .zshrc and similar

Cause. --tui was run with neither installed. Fix. Install one, or accept the offered fallback to the CLI menu. sudo apt install whiptail # Debian / Ubuntu sudo dnf install newt # Fedora / RHEL sudo pacman -S libnewt # Arch Verify. command -v whiptail, then re-run. See TUI.
documents.s: TUI mode needs whiptail or dialog

documents.t: Cause. --export md, --export html, or a conversion in the reports manager, without jq installed. Fix. sudo apt install jq jq is needed only for conversion. JSON records are still written on every run without it. See Reports.

Cause. A required dependency is missing or shadowed by an incompatible alias. Common on minimal containers that ship BusyBox instead of GNU coreutils. Verify. linux-cleanup --self-test This probes every required command and names the first one missing. Fix. Install your distro's coreutils, findutils and gawk packages. On Alpine: apk add coreutils findutils bash realpath matters most — it is what makes the protected-path check symlink-safe. See Distro support.

Verify. tail -100 ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log crontab -l | grep -i cleanup Cause. command not found in the cron log means cron's minimal PATH (/usr/bin:/bin) cannot see your install. This is the single most common cron problem. Fix. Use an absolute path in the crontab: crontab -e # Change: 0 3 * * 0 linux-cleanup --all-safe -y … # To: 0 3 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/linux-cleanup --all-safe -y … Find the right path with command -v linux-cleanup. Alternatively put a PATH= line at the top of the crontab. See Alias and cron.
documents.s: Cron entry runs but does nothing

documents.t: ✗ $HOME is not set Cause. Running in a context that does not set $HOME — some Docker images, some CI runners. Fix. HOME=/root linux-cleanup --scan Or export it once for the session. The script aborts rather than guessing, deliberately: a wrong $HOME would mean every path check is evaluated against the wrong tree.

Cause. find walking thousands of directories under $HOME. On a spinning disk the first run takes one to three minutes. Verify. Watch the log rather than the terminal: tail -f ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-*.log New lines every five to ten seconds means it is working. Fix. Be patient on the first run; later runs are faster thanks to cached directory metadata. If the same path consistently stalls past five minutes, suspect a symlink loop or an unresponsive network or FUSE mount — and report it.

Cause. The reported recovery is a df delta across the whole machine. Another process — a build, a package update, journal rotation, an IDE re-indexing — wrote more during your session than the cleanup reclaimed. This is not a bug, and it does not mean the cleanup failed. Check what the steps themselves reported: jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran") | {title, freed_bytes}' \ "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" Fix. Re-run --scan when the machine is quiet to see the real picture.
documents.s: Disk usage grew during the session

documents.t: Cause. Rare. apt clean does not break apt update, but the cleanup may have raced with another apt operation holding a lock. Verify. sudo apt update 2>&1 | tail -20 Fix. sudo rm -f /var/lib/apt/lists/lock /var/cache/apt/archives/lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend sudo apt update Do this only when no apt process is genuinely running — ps aux | grep -i apt first.

Cause. Usually correct behaviour: a superseded version was removed while the editor still held a reference to it. Fix. Reload the window — Ctrl+Shift+P → Developer: Reload Window. Verify the current version is still present: ls ~/.vscode/extensions/ | grep <extension-name> If the current version is genuinely gone, that indicates a bug in the highest-version detection. Reinstall and report it: code --install-extension <publisher>.<name>
documents.s: VS Code reports a missing extension

documents.t: Cause. The script exited non-zero from somewhere unexpected — a backgrounded find killed by the OOM killer, or a broken pipe. Fix. Read the exit code in the bundle's manifest: tar -xzOf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/crash-*.tar.gz --wildcards '*MANIFEST*' 137 is the OOM killer, 141 is SIGPIPE, 139 a segfault. See Exit codes. Any of these is worth reporting.
documents.s: A crash bundle appeared but I saw no crash

documents.t: Cause. The shell rc file has not been re-read. Fix. source ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc Or open a new terminal.

Verify. command -v linux-cleanup linux-cleanup --version Cause. An old global install shadowing a newer npx cache, or a stale shell command hash. Fix. npm uninstall -g linux-cleanup npm install -g linux-cleanup@latest hash -r linux-cleanup --version The npm registry reported 1.6.0 on 2026-10-14. Review the changelog for fixes since 1.4.0.
linux-cleanup --debug-bundle linux-cleanup --feedback Review the bundle, then email it with a short description of expected versus actual. See Send a bug report.
